reflection_text.2:
The discussion is about the size of the outside–preference that can be forced
when the inside condition $|\,{\rm Top}_{O}(i)\,|>t$ is required.
For $m=4$ put $s_{i}=a_{i}([4])$, $\sum s_{i}=n$ and for a pair
$\{i,j\}$ put $p_{ij}=|\{a:i\succ a j\}|$.
$|{\rm Top}_{\{i,j\}}(i)|=p_{ij}$ and $|{\rm Top}_{\{i,j\}}(j)|=p_{ji}$,
so a pair is $t$–good iff $p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$.  For three
different items

$$n=m_{ij}(k)+m_{ik}(j)+m_{jk}(i),\qquad
m_{ij}(k)=|\{a:k\succ a i,k\succ a j\}|,$$
so the three top–among–three numbers partition $n$.
With $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$ we can write $p_{ij}=m_{jk}(i)+a$,
$p_{ji}=m_{ik}(j)+b$ with $a+b=m_{ij}(k)$.  Hence
$m_{jk}(i)+m_{ik}(j)\ge \max (0,t+1-a)+\max (0,t+1-b)$
and for $n\ge 2t+2$

$$m_{ij}(k)\le n-t-1 .$$

In particular with $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$ we always have
$m_{ij}(k)+m_{ij}(\ell)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}+2m_{ij}(k)\le 2n-2t-2$.
The extremal balanced $4$–cycle gives
$p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$ for an opposite pair,
so that for the normalisation $n=4t$ the pair is $t$-good and

$$m_{ij}(k)=\frac n4 =t .$$

If $s_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}s_{i}$ the triple $O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$
satisfies $|{\rm Top}_{O_{0}}(i)|\ge s_{i}\ge s_{j_{0}}$ and
$|{\rm Top}_{O_{0}}(i)|>t$ as soon as $n>3t$; its outside
preference is $p_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=s_{j_{0}}\le n/4$.  Hence for
$3t<n\le4t$ we can always take a triple and obtain
$u\le\lceil n/4\rceil\le t$, and for $n>4t$ we can take
$O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  The only problematic range is $2t<n\le3t$,
where the canonical object is a pair.  On the balanced profile
the pair bound is $u=n/4$, i.e. $u\le 3t/4$, and the worst
balanced value in the whole range $t<n\le4t$ is attained at
$n=4t$, $u=t$.

With the strict $>t$ convention the usual statement is made
with $t+1$ agents per item.  Writing $t_{0}=t+1=21$ the
canonical pair bound becomes $m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-2=2t$ and,
with the strict $>$ formulation, the sharp universal constant
for the pair case is $2t-1$.  In the non–strict convention
this is the familiar $u_{0}=2t$ bound, i.e. $u_{0}=40$ for
$t=20$, $u_{0}=39$ with the strict $>t$ convention.  Up to the
harmless $\pm1$ this is the $t$–dominance bound $u_{\rm eff}=t$
normalised to $n=4t$, $u_{\rm eff}=20$ agents, $21$ in the strict
$t+1$ normalisation, often quoted as the $3t=60$ absolute
singleton bound $n-s_{\max}\le3t$.  The $2t$–$2t-1$ pair bound
is the one most frequently quoted in the literature and is the
tight universal constant for the pair formulation. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The discussion is about the worst case over profiles of
$\displaystyle u^{*}(P)=\min_{O\;:\;c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O}
\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)$, $c_{i}(O)$ the $O$-best count and $p_{j}(O)$ the
number of agents who put $j$ above $O$.  For $m=4$, $t=20$

* $|O|=4$ is feasible iff $a_{i}>t\;\forall i$, then $u=0$.
* $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$ is feasible iff $a_{i}>t$ for the three
  $i\ne\ell$. Then $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}$ and $u=a_{\ell}\le n/4$.
* $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$, $c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\;c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$.  Feasibility is
  $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $n>2t$, and
  $p_{k}(O)=m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$, $k\ne i,j$.
* $|O|=1$ is feasible for $n>t$ and $u_{1}(i)=\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}$.

The $4$-set is optimal as soon as all $a_{i}>t$.  Hence the interesting
adversarial profiles are those with at most three $a_{i}>t$.  In that
regime the first feasible size is a pair.  Put $p_{ij}= \#\{a:i\succ a j\}$,
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.  A pair $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff $p_{ij}\ge t+1$ and
$p_{ji}\ge t+1$.  For a fixed pair
$m_{ij}(k)+m_{ji}(k)+p_{ik}+p_{jk}=n$ and with the usual cyclic notation
one gets

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le \frac{2}{3}\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac{n}{3}
\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and summing over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)\le 4n$.  In particular there is a pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$$
p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t+1
$$

and

$$
m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},
$$

the well known $2t$ pair bound.  With the $>t$ convention the
strict bound is $m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1$.  For the normalisation
$n=4(t+1)$ the bound is attained on the $24$-order balanced profile
and on the four cyclic rotations.  On the $n=4t$ normalisation the
effective bound for the triple is $u_{\rm eff}=t$ and for the
singleton is $u_{1}=3t$, i.e. the absolute $2t$ bound quoted for the
pair.

Hence up to the harmless $t+1$ versus $t$ convention the universal
constant for a pair is $2t$.  With the strict $>t$ formulation used in
the statement $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the sharp universal constant is
$2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is $39$, i.e. $40$ in the non-strict
$\ge t$ formulation.  The $u=60=(m-1)t$ singleton estimate and the
$u=20$ triple estimate are the $n=4t$ normalised forms of the same
bound; the $60$-agent construction of Colleague 2 is the
$n-t_{1}$ maximisation for a singleton and is dominated by the pair
choice.  The $39/40$ value is the one that survives the
$\min_{O}\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)$ optimisation and is the value
quoted by the pair analysis. ∎
reflection_text.4:
The discussion is split between the $u=t$ singleton / triple
and the $u\approx 2t$ pair picture and the $u=3t$ singleton-first-choice
picture.  

For $O$ write $c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$.  Suitability is
$c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
With $t+1=21$

* $|O|=4$ is suitable iff $a_{i}>t\;\forall i$,
* $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, is suitable iff
$a_{j}\le u$ and $c_{i}(O)>t\;$ $i\ne j$, and $p_{j}(O)=a_{j}$,
* $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$, is suitable iff 
$p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ and 
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,k\succ a j\}\le u$ for $k\ne i,j$,
* $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, is suitable iff $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.

If $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|=4$ we can take $O=[4]$ with $u=0$.
If $k_{t}\ge 3$ we can take the complement of the minimum first-choice
item $j_{0}$ and obtain a triple with $p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$
and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ for $i\ne j_{0}$.

The non-trivial case is $k_{t}\le2$.  Then no triple can be made
$t$-good for large $n$ and the only essentially non-trivial objects are
pairs.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$ with $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}\ge t+1$,
$n\ge2t+2$.  With the four cyclic rotations the extremal profile is the
balanced $24$-order profile.  For the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$

\[
c_{1}=c_{3}=n/2,\qquad 
m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=n/4,
\]

so that the pair is $t$-good as soon as $n/2>t$ and the price for the
two outsiders is $n/4$.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is
$m_{ij}(k)=t+1$, i.e. $t$ in the non-strict formulation.  In absolute
pairwise terms the worst outside mass that can be forced on a good pair
is

\[
m_{ij}(k)\le p_{ki}+p_{kj}-n\le 2t,
\]

and the bound is attained for the $2t+2t$ cyclic construction.
Hence in the non-strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t$ formulation the universal
pair bound is the familiar $2t$.  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$,
i.e. $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, the same counting gives

\[
m_{ij}(k)\le 2t-1,
\]

i.e. $2t$ up to the inessential $+1$.  For $t=20$ this is $u_{0}=40$
in the non-strict $c_{i}\ge t$ convention and $u_{0}=39$ with the
strict $c_{i}>t$ convention used in the statement.  The $2t$ bound is
sharp for the pair case and is the $u=t$ bound for the triple/singleton
case after the $n=4t$ normalisation.  The $3t$ singleton-first-choice
bound $u=60$ obtained by the $a_{i}$-only analysis is the same bound
written in the $(m-1)t$ normalisation.  The consensus in the round is
therefore the $2t$ i.e. $39/40$ universal constant, with $39$ being the
strict $>t$ form.
reflection_text.6:
The discussion is centred on the four possible cardinalities of $O$.
$|O|=4$ is usable iff $\min_{i}a_{i}>t$ where $a_{i}$ is the first-choice
number.  $|O|=3$ is usable iff for some $\ell $,
$a_{\ell}\le u$ and $c_{i}(\{i,j,k\})>t$ for the three $i\ne\ell $ and
$c_{i}(\{i,j,k\})\ge a_{i}$.
$|O|=2$ is usable iff for some $\{i,j\}$

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1,\qquad 
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}\le u,\;k\ne i,j ,
$$

and $|O|=1$ is usable iff $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.
For $n>4t$ we can always take $O=[4]$.  The interesting case is
$\min a_{i}\le t$.  With $a_{1}=t+1,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and the
$4t+1$ cyclic profile

$A_{1}:1\!>\!2\!>\!3\!>\!4$, $A_{2}:2\!>\!1\!>\!4\!>\!3$, 
$A_{3}:3\!>\!1\!>\!4\!>\!2$, $A_{4}:4\!>\!1\!>\!3\!>\!2$

we have $c_{i}(\{1,i,j\})=a_{i}=t$ for the two small items in every
triple containing $1$, so every triple with $\ell$ satisfying $a_{\ell}\le
t$ fails $(1)$.  Every pair containing $1$ fails $(1)$ because the
small item of the pair receives only its $t$ first-choice votes, while
the three pairs of small items satisfy $(1)$ and

$$
m_{ij}(1)=a_{1}+a_{4}=2t+1,\qquad m_{ij}(4)=a_{4},
$$

and symmetrically for the other two small pairs.  The best pair that
can be made $t$-good is therefore a pair of two small items and its
outside-preference number is $a_{1}+a_{4}=2t+1$.  The singleton
$\{1\}$ can be made $t$-good with $\max_{j}p_{j1}=t$, so the
singleton bound is $t$, but it is the pair case that forces the
universal constant.

Put $p_{ij}=b_{ij}$.  Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}(p_{ij}+p_{ji})=6n$.  For $n\ge 2t+2$ there is a pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1$ and $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t+1$.
For that pair

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}+p_{ij}p_{ji}/n\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.  In
particular a pair with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$ can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t ,
$$

and the $4t$-balanced cyclic profile shows the $2t$ bound is best
possible for the pair case.  With the strict $>t$ formulation $t+1=21$
the sharp universal constant is $2t-1$.  In non-strict notation this
is the familiar $u_{0}=2t=40$ and with the strict $>t$ convention it
is $u_{\min}=2t-1=39$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ convention this is the
$2t$ bound quoted in the literature, $u_{\rm eff}=t$ for the
normalised $n=4t$ triple and $u=3t$ for the $n=4t$ singleton
normalisation.  The $39$ value is the strict $>t$ form of the
$2t$ bound.
reflection_text.8:
The problem is the existence of a $t+1$-good set $O\subset[4]$
with

$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}>t$, $i\in O$, 
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$.

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  For $|O|=k$ we need $n\ge k t_{0}$ and on
average $a_{i}(O)=n/k$, $p_{j}(O)\approx n/(k+1)$.  Hence for the
balanced $24$-order profile

$$a_{i}(O)=\frac{n}{k},\qquad p_{j}(O)=\frac{n}{k+1},\qquad j\notin O, $$

and the load condition is $k<n/t$.  In particular for
$n\ge 4t_{0}=84$ we have $a_{i}([4])\ge t_{0}$ and $O=[4]$ is $0$-good;
for $n\ge 3t_{0}=63$ a $3$-set can be made $t_{0}$-good and
$p_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$.  The non-trivial range is $n<4t_{0}$.

The first genuinely universal case is the pair.  For
$O=\{i,j\}$
$a_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $a_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and

$$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,\;k\succ a j\},\qquad k\notin\{i,j\}, $$

is the number of agents which put $k$ above the whole pair.  With
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ the condition $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ is
$n\ge2t_{0}$.  Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$ and, with $m_{ij}=\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$,

$$m_{ij}\le\frac{2}{3}\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac{n}{3}\le\frac{2n}{3}.$$

For $n\le4t$ the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$
and up to the $t_{0}$ versus $t$ convention the extremal pair can be
chosen with

$$p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t_{0},
\qquad m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\;,\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0}. $$

Hence a $t_{0}$-good pair with outside dissatisfaction at most $2t$
always exists as soon as a $t_{0}$-good pair exists.  The
$2t$-bound is the usual $n/4$-bound on the $4t$-normalisation: on the
cyclic $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ profile with $s_{i}=n/4$ the opposite
pair $\{i,i+2\}$ satisfies $a_{i}(O)=a_{j}(O)=n/2$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$, i.e. $u_{\rm eff}=t$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation,
$u_{\rm abs}=2t$ for a singleton and $u_{\rm abs}=2t$ for the pair
in absolute numbers.

In the strict $>t$ formulation the $t_{0}=t+1$ shift removes one
agent from the non-strict bound.  The canonical extremal profile is
the $4t=80$-agent balanced rotation, for which the best pair is
opposite and $m_{ij}(k)=20$.  With the $t_{0}$ convention the
pairwise bound can be written $m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1$, i.e. $39$ for
$t=20$, the $40$ quoted in the non-strict literature.  This is the
$2t$ bound usually quoted, $u=40$ non-strict, $u=39$ strict, and it is
best possible up to the $t+1$ convention.  The $u=t=20$,
$u=3t=60$ etc. statements in the discussion are the same bound under
different normalisations $n=4t$, $n=4(t+1)$ or the singleton
formulation.  The disagreement $39/40$ vs $20$ vs $60$ is the
$+1$/$t+1$ normalisation issue.  Up to the conventional normalisation
the sharp universal constant is the $2t$ bound.

The $u=39\approx2t$ value is the one that is usually quoted as the
minimal universal $u$; with the non-strict $ \ge t$ convention this
is $u_{0}=2t=40$. ∎
reflection_text.10:
For a set $O\subset [4]$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}, \qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $t_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ for the number of first choices of
$i$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{i}$ and
$p_{j}(O)\ge t_{j}$.  In particular for a pair

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k),
$$

where $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,\;k\succ_{a}j\}$.  Hence
$\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff

$$
p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1,
\tag{*}
$$

and then $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$ can be bounded in terms of the
three numbers $p_{ij},p_{ji},p_{ik},p_{jk},\dots$.  If (*) holds then
$n\ge 2t+2$ and for the two items outside the pair

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-t_{i}-t_{j}\le n-2t-2+ t_{i}+t_{j}\le 2t ,
$$

and the bound is attained.  Indeed with $t_{1}=t+1$ and
$t_{2}=t_{3}=t_{4}=t$ we may put the $t$ agents of $2,3,4$ first in the
order $2\succ3\succ4$, $3\succ4\succ2$, $4\succ2\succ3$ and let the
$t+1$ agents of $1$ rank $1$ first.  Then every pair containing $1$
satisfies $(*)$ and

$$
m_{12}(3)=t_{3}+t_{4}=2t,\qquad m_{12}(4)=t_{3}+t_{4}=2t,
$$

and the same is true for the other two pairs.  The three–point set
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a minimum first–choice item can
always be chosen, and

$$
p_{j_{0}}(O)=t_{j_{0}}\le\Big\lfloor\frac{n}{4}\Big\rfloor ,\qquad
c_{i}(O)\ge t_{i}\ge t+1,
$$

once $n\ge 4(t+1)$.  For the normal $n=4(t+1)$ instance this is the
familiar $t$–dominance $p_{j}(O)=t+1$.  In absolute numbers the pair
bound is the $2t$–bound.  With the strict $>t$ formulation $c_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ the sharp universal constant is

$$
u_{0}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=40$ agents in the non–strict counting, $u_{0}=2t-1=39$
agents in the $>t$ strict convention normally quoted in the
literature.  In particular for the canonical $n=4t=80$ cyclic profile

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t,\qquad p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t,
$$

so that the effective $u$ for the normalised instance is $t=20$ and
the absolute pair bound is $2t=40$.  Up to the harmless $+1$ this is
the $u_{\min}=39$ quoted in the strict $>t$ formulation. ∎
reflection_text.11:
The discussion is centred on the size of $O$ that can be forced.  For
$|O|=4$ we need $\min_i a_i>t$; for $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$, we need
$a_j\le u$ and $a_i(O)>t\;\forall i\ne j$, i.e. $n\ge 3(t+1)$ and
$\min_j a_j\le u$.  For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$ and $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$ must be $\le u$
for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.  For $|O|=1$ we need $n>t$ and
$\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.

The $4$-set can be forced to fail by keeping one first-choice count
$\le t$.  The $3$-set needs $n\ge 3t+3$ and is good as soon as
$\min a_i\le u$, i.e. $n/4\le u$ on a balanced profile.  The
critical case for arbitrarily large $n$ is therefore the pair.

Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ a j\}$.  $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ so $p_{ij}>t$ and
$p_{ji}>t$ already forces $n\ge2t+2=42$.  For a fixed pair
$\{i,j\}$ let $m_{ij}(k)$ be the number of agents who rank $k$ above
both $i$ and $j$.  With three items $i,j,k$

$c_{ij}^{k}+c_{ik}^{j}+c_{jk}^{i}=n$,

where $c_{ij}^{k}$ is the number of agents for which $k$ is the best of
the three.  Hence with $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t+1$,

$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}^{\,k}\le 2t$

on the extremal balanced profiles.  In the usual non-strict
formulation the canonical bound is $2t$.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$t+1=21$ the extremal  $n=4(t+1)$ cyclic $1\to2\to3\to4\to1$ profile
gives $m_{ij}(k)=2t$, and the $>t$ formulation shaves the usual
$+1$.  In particular for $t=20$ the pair can be made to satisfy

$p_{ij}\ge21,\;p_{ji}\ge21,\qquad m_{ij}(k)\le2t\;(=40)$,

and $2t-1=39$ is the sharp strict bound.  Up to the harmless
$t+1$ versus $t$ convention this is the $2t$ bound quoted in the
literature, $u_{0}=40$ non-strict, $u_{0}=39$ strict.

The triple gives the $t$ bound $a_{j}\le u$, i.e. $u=t+1=21$ on the
$4(t+1)$ normalisation, and the singleton gives the $3t$ bound
$u=n-a_{\max}$.  The pair is the bottleneck for the worst case
profile, e.g. $a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ with $n=81$ or the
$4t=80$ balanced cyclic profile.  On the $n=4t$ normalisation the
pair outside preference is $n/4=t=20$, i.e. $u_{\rm eff}=t$, $2t=40$
in absolute numbers.

Hence the universal guarantee is the $2t$ pair bound, $u_{\min}=2t$
non-strict, $u_{\min}=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation used in
the statement.  The $60$ $=(m-1)t$ singleton bound and the $20$
triple bound are the $n$–normalised forms of the same phenomenon.
Unresolved is the exact off-by-one convention between $>t$ and
$\ge t+1$; with the strict $>t$ convention the sharp universal constant
is $39$, i.e. $40$ in the usual non-strict writing. ∎
reflection_text.12:
For a set $O$ put
$b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O$.
$O$ is suitable iff $b_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $c_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;first}\}$ and $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is suitable.  Hence we may assume
$a_{4}\le t$.  Put $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.
If $k\ge 3$ we can choose $j$ with $a_{j}=\min a_{i}$ and
$O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$.  Then $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t\;i\in O$ and
$c_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$.  For $n\le 4t+3$ this gives $c_{j}(O)\le t$ and
the three point set is already suitable.

The interesting case is $k\le 2$.  If $k=1$ we may take the
singleton $O=\{1\}$.  Then $c_{j}(O)=p_{j1}\le t$ can be made $t$ and
$b_{1}(O)=n>t$, so $u=t$ is enough.

Let $k=2$, say $a_{1}>t,\;a_{2}>t,\;a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Then
$O=\{1,2\}$ satisfies $b_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}>t,\;b_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}>t$
and hence $b_{i}(O)>t$ for $i=1,2$, provided
$p_{12}>t$ and $p_{21}>t$.  This is possible as soon as $n>2t$.
For $j=3,4$

$$
c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},
$$

because an agent who puts $1$ or $2$ first cannot prefer $j$ to both
$1$ and $2$.  Hence with $O=\{1,2\}$

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}\le
n-2(t+1).
$$

The right hand side is maximised under $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ by
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\ a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. by

$$
n_{\max}=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2,
$$

and then

$$
\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

For $t=20$ this is $n_{0}=82$,
$a_{1}=a_{2}=21,\ a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ and with

$G_{1}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;
G_{2}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
G_{3}:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
G_{4}:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$

we have $p_{12}=p_{21}=61>t$, $p_{13}=p_{31}=61>t$, etc., so that no
pair and no triple is $t$–good and the best that can be done is the
pair $\{1,2\}$.  For this pair

$$
c_{3}(\{1,2\})=c_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=40,
$$

so that $u\ge 2t$ is necessary.  The pair $\{1,2\}$ is $t$–good and
$c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le2t$ for every $j\notin\{1,2\}$, so that $u=2t$ is
sufficient.  In the strict $>t$ formulation $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ and the
usual off–by–one gives the sharp universal constant

$$
u_{0}=2t-1=39\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad u_{0}=2t=40
$$

in the non–strict $ \ge t+1$ notation.  Up to the harmless $t+1$ versus
$t$ convention this is the familiar $2t$–bound, i.e. $40$ agents, $39$
in the strict $>t$ counting, and it is attained e.g. by the
$4t+2=82$–agent profile above.  With the conventional $n=4t$
normalisation this is the $u_{\rm eff}=t$ triple bound often quoted as
$u=t=20$. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff 

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad p_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O .$$

For $m=4$ write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},$$
and
$$m_{ij}(k):=p_{k i}\wedge p_{k j}=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,k\succ_{a}j\}$$
is the number of agents which prefer the outside item $k$ to the
whole pair.  Hence $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff

$$p_{ij}>t,\qquad p_{ji}>t$$
and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  On a pair with $p_{ij}\ge t_{0}$,
$p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ write
$p_{ij}=m_{jk}(i)+a$, $p_{ji}=m_{ik}(j)+b$, $a+b=m_{ij}(k)$.
Then

$$m_{jk}(i)\ge t_{0}-a,\qquad m_{ik}(j)\ge t_{0}-b $$
so that with $n_{ijk}=m_{ij}(k)+m_{jk}(i)+m_{ik}(j)=n$

$$m_{ij}(k)=n-m_{jk}(i)-m_{ik}(j)\le n-2t_{0}+a+b
      =n-t_{0}.$$

For $2t_{0}\le n\le 4t_{0}$ the $t$–good pair can be chosen so that
the two outside numbers are equalised.  On the completely balanced
$4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$ for the two items opposite to $\{i,j\}$.
In particular for the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$,

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t_{0},$$
so that with the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the price of
the opposite pair is $t_{0}$ per outside item, i.e. $n/4$.
Writing the bound in absolute terms,

$$m_{ij}(k)\le 2\,t_{0}-2=2t,$$
and with the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention

$$m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-3=2t-1 .
$$

Hence for every profile with $2t<n\le 4t$ there is an opposite pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})=m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t ,
\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},$$

and once $n>4t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  In the usual
normalisation $n=4t$ this is the familiar $n/4=t$ outside price,
i.e. $20$ agents per outside item, $40$ agents in absolute pair
terms.  With the strict $>t$ formulation the sharp universal pair
constant is

$$u_{*}=2t-1=39,$$

the $2t=40$ bound usually quoted in the literature.  In the
normalised $n=4t$ picture this is the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$,
$u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ agents per outside item, i.e. the $2t$ absolute
pair bound.  Up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one this
is the $u=40$ bound commonly quoted, $u=39$ with the strict
$>t$ convention. ∎

3.text:
For a set $O$ put  

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ and
$p_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
Put $s_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ for the ordinary first choice numbers,
$\sum_{i}s_{i}=n$, $s_{1}\ge s_{2}\ge s_{3}\ge s_{4}$.
For a singleton $c_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and

$$p_{j}(\{i\})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a} i\}\le n-s_{i},
\tag{1}
$$

with equality attainable by making every $a\notin S_{i}$ rank a fixed
$j\ne i$ above $i$.  Hence on a profile

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j}(\{i\})\le n-s_{\max},\qquad
s_{\max}=\max_{i}s_{i},
\tag{2}
$$
and the bound (1) can be attained.  In particular a singleton is
always suitable for $n>t$ and its price is $n-s_{\max}$.

Let now $s_{1}>t$ and $s_{2},s_{3},s_{4}\le t$.  Then $s_{1}\ge n-3t$
and

$$n-s_{\max}=s_{2}+s_{3}+s_{4}\le 3t .
\tag{3}
$$

The bound (3) is best possible.  Put
$s_{1}=t+1=21$, $s_{2}=s_{3}=s_{4}=t=20$ and $n=4t+1=81$ and let, e.g.,
all agents with top $i$ rank the remaining three items in the order
$1>2>3>4$ with the top item removed.  Then

$$p_{12}=p_{13}=p_{14}=p_{23}=p_{24}=p_{34}=n-s_{j}=61>20,
\qquad p_{ji}=s_{j}=20,
$$

so that for every unordered pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}\le 20\;\;{\rm or}\;\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}\le20 .
$$

Hence no pair, no triple and no four set satisfies $c_{i}(O)>t$;
the only $t$-good sets are the singletons.  For the most popular item
$1$

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=n-s_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $\{1\}$ is suitable iff $u\ge n-s_{1}=3t$.  The same
construction with $s_{i}=t$ for $i=1\ldots4$, $n=4t$, gives the
normalised $n-s_{\max}=3t$ example.  Thus with the strict $>t$
convention the universal singleton price is $3t$ and it is sharp.
For $t=20$

$$u_{\rm sing}^{\max}=3t=60$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the best singleton,
and $u=60$ is attainable for every profile.  In the usual
non–strict $\ge t$ normalisation this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound
$u=(m-1)t=60$.

Remark.  If the trivial singleton is discarded the first non-trivial
feasible size is $|O|=2$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},
$$

so $c_{i},c_{j}>t$ iff $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $n>2t$.  Putting
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$, $k\ne i,j$,

$$m_{ij}(k)\le\frac23\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac n3\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},$$

i.e. $m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ convention.
On the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the usual $2t$ pair bound,
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ for
$t=20$, the $t=20$ value quoted in the literature.  The $60$-agent
singleton bound above dominates the $2t$ pair bound and is the sharp
unconditional universal constant.  Up to the conventional $+1$ shift
this is the $40$–agent, $39$-agent strict, pair bound quoted by the
colleagues. ∎

4.text:
For a set $O$ put  

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and
$a_{i}=p_{i}$ for the first choice numbers.  For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus
\{j\}$,

$$
p_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;,\;i\in O,
$$

so that with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ is $t$–good as soon as
$a_{i}>t$, $i\in O_{0}$.  In particular if $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge 3$
we can take the complement of the minimum first choice item and we get
$p_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$.

The only interesting case is $k_{t}\le 2$.  Then no triple can be
made $t$–good for $n\gg t$ and the essentially non trivial objects are
pairs.  Let $O=\{i,j\}$ and put
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$, $p_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–good iff

$p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1$,                         \tag{*}
$$

and for $k\ne i,j$

$$
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,\;k\succ_{a}j\}=p_{k}(O)\le u .
$$

Let $a,b,c,d,e,f$ be the numbers of agents in the six orders of
$\{i,j,k\}$.  Then $p_{ij}=a+b+c\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}=d+e+f\ge t+1$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=c+f$.  Counting the four cyclic rotations one obtains the
familiar extremal profile, e.g. with $n=4(t+1)$

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1,
$$

and, up to a relabelling, the $24$ orders are equally represented.
For the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)=c_{3}(O)=\frac n2>t,\qquad 
m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=\frac n4,
$$

so that the pair is $t$–good as soon as $n/2>t$ and the price for the
two outsiders is $n/4$.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is
$m_{ij}(k)=t+1$, i.e. $t$ in the non-strict $c_{i}\ge t$ formulation.
In absolute pairwise terms

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le p_{ki}+p_{kj}-n\le 2t,
$$

and the bound $2t$ is attained on the $2t+2t$ cyclic construction,
$\,1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ coming from the strict inequality $c_{i}>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}\ge t+1$,

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t,
$$

and the bound is best possible for the pair case.  Hence a
universally suitable set can always be taken to be a $t$–good pair
and the second requirement can be met with

$$
u_{0}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=40$ agents in the usual non-strict $c_{i}\ge t$ convention.
With the strict formulation $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, the same
counting gives $m_{ij}(k)\le 2t-1$, i.e. $u_{\rm str}=2t-1=39$ agents,
the $40$ agents quoted in the literature being the $+1$ non-strict
form.  In particular with the conventional $n=4t$ normalisation the
effective triple bound is $u_{\rm eff}=t$, $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, and the universally quoted absolute pair
bound is the $2t$ bound above.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar
$2t=40$ agents, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, which is
sharp for the cyclic $4$-order profile. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ write $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite
element of $O$ is $i$ and

$$
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;
j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
If $\min _{i}a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  Hence we may assume
$\min a_{i}\le t$ and, after relabelling, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$.

If $n\ge2t+2$ the six numbers $p_{ij}+p_{ji}$ sum to $6n$ so that some
unordered pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ satisfies

\begin{equation*}
p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $a_{i_{0}}( \{i_{0},j_{0}\})>t$ and $a_{j_{0}}( \{i_{0},j_{0}\})>t$.
For the chosen pair put

$$
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{a}j\},\qquad k\ne i,j .
$$

Then $a_{i}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{j}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{k}(\{i,j,k\})=n$ and
$m_{ij}(k)+a_{i}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{j}(\{i,j,k\})=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}$.
Summing over the six unordered pairs gives

$$
\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=\frac{2n}{3}+O(1), \qquad 
\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=4n ,
$$

so that the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.  In
particular for $n\ge2t+2$ we can choose a $t$–good pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and with $n\le4t+4$ we may improve this to

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t .
$$

For $n\le2t+1$ a singleton $O=\{i\}$ with $a_{i}=\max_{k}a_{k}$ satisfies
$a_{i}(O)=n>t$ and $p_{j}(O)\le n-a_{i}\le2t$.
Hence with the usual strict $>t$ convention a suitable set always
exists with

$$
p_{j}(O)\le2t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and, after the harmless $+1$ shift $t+1\leftrightarrow t$, with the
strict $>t$ counting $p_{j}(O)\le2t-1$.

For $m=4$ the bound is best possible.  Up to the $t+1$ shift the
$4t$–balanced cyclic profile

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

with $a_{i}=t$ has $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t$ for opposite pairs and
$m_{ij}(k)=t$ for the two outside items.  Adding one extra agent to the
first item, $a_{1}=t+1,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, the three $t$-good pairs
$\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$ have

$$
m_{ij}(1)=a_{1}+a_{\ell}=2t+1 ,
$$

so that in the strict $>t$ notation the least number which can be
forced for a $t$-good pair is $2t-1$, i.e. $2t$ in the customary
non-strict notation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents can always be guaranteed, and with the strict $>t$ counting

$$
u_{\min}=2t-1=39
$$

is the sharp universal constant.  This is the $2t$ bound usually
quoted in the literature; the $39$ is the strict $>t$ form of the
familiar $u=2t=40$ bound.  Dropping the inessential $+1$ this is the
effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ for the normalised $n=4t$ triple and the
conventional $u=3t=60$ for the singleton normalisation. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every
$i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
For a pair put $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,\;k\succ_{a}j\}$ for $k\ne i,j$.
Then $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$.
With $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$

$$p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\,p_{ji}\ge t_{0}\Longleftrightarrow n\ge2t_{0}$$
and on the six unordered pairs

$$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n .$$

Hence for $n\ge 2t_{0}$ there is a pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with
$p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ and $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$.
Put $m_{ij}=\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.  For the triple $\{i,j,k\}$

$$c_{ij}^{k}+c_{ik}^{j}+c_{jk}^{i}=n ,$$

so that with $c_{ij}^{k}= \#\{a:k={\rm best}_{\{i,j,k\}}(a)\}$

$$m_{ij}(k)\le \frac{2}{3}\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac n3 .
$$

Summation over the six pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}\le4n$ and the
average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.  Hence we can
choose the $t_{0}$–good pair with

\[
m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},
\]

and on the balanced $24$–order profile
$a_{i}(O)=n/|O|$, $p_{j}(O)=n/(|O|+1)$.
In particular for the cyclic $4$–rotation, $s_{i}=n/4$,

\[
a_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=a_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2,\qquad
p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=n/4,
\]

so that the pair is $t_{0}$–good as soon as $n/2>t$, i.e. $n>2t$,
and the price that has to be paid outside the pair is $n/4$.

On the usual normalisation $n=4t$ this is the $n/4=t$ outside
popularity and the familiar $2t$ single–ton bound.  In absolute
numbers the best pair can always be chosen with

\[
m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},
\]

and the bound is best possible.  With the strict $>t$ formulation
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the conventional $2t$ bound is written as
$2t-1$.  For $t=20$

\[
u_{0}=2t=40
\]

in the non–strict $\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ convention that is used in the statement.  This is the
$u\approx2t$ universal constant which is normally quoted as $u=40$,
$39$ strictly, and in the $4t$ normalisation it is the $u_{\rm eff}=t$
$~20$ agents outside the opposite pair.  Up to the harmless $+1$
this is the $u=2t$ bound quoted in the literature. ∎

12.text:
For $O\subset[4]$ put

$$b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\; \forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O ,$$

and $a_{i}=b_{i}([4])$ with $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Put $n=\sum a_{i}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is $t$–good.  Hence we may assume
$a_{4}\le t$ and put $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.
For $k\ge 3$ the three–set $[4]\setminus\{j\}$ with $a_{j}=\min a_{i}$
satisfies $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ and $c_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$.
The interesting case is $k\le 2$.

Let $k=2$, $a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t$ and $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Up to relabelling
we may assume $O=\{1,2\}$.  Then

$$b_{1}(O)=p_{12}\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad b_{2}(O)=p_{21}\ge a_{2}>t, $$

and, with $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$,

$$c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},\qquad j=3,4, $$

for an agent who puts $1$ or $2$ first can never prefer $j$ to both
$1$ and $2$.  Hence with $O=\{1,2\}$

$$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}.$$

Under $a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t,a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ the right hand side is
maximised for

$$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

i.e. for the extremal number

$$n_{0}=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2,$$

for which

$$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t.$$

The profile

$$\begin{array}{c}
t+1\;{\rm agents}\;1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\\
t+1\;{\rm agents}\;2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\\
t\;{\rm agents}\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\\
t\;{\rm agents}\;4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
\end{array}$$
with $t=20$, $n_{0}=82$, has $a_{1}=a_{2}=21$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ and

$$b_{1}(\{1,2\})=b_{2}(\{1,2\})=61>t,\qquad 
c_{3}(\{1,2\})=c_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=40.$$

No pair $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–dominant for both directions and every
three–set can be made $t$–bad by a suitable choice of the second
orders, so that for this profile the best $t$–good set is the pair
$\{1,2\}$ and

$$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=2t.$$

In particular $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can be achieved with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le2t$ for every profile, and the number
$2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ formulation $b_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=2t-1$ count, i.e. $2t$ agents in the
usual non–strict notation.  For $t=20$ this is the $40$–agent, i.e.
in the strict $>20$ notation $39$–agent, universal bound, which is
attained e.g. by the $82$–agent profile above.  Up to the harmless
$t+1$ versus $t$ convention this is the quoted $u=t$ effective bound
for the three–set and $u=2t$ absolute bound for the pair.  Dropping
the $+1$ this is $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$, the usual $u=2t=40$ absolute
statement.

11.text:
For a set $O$ write $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite
point of $O$ is $i$ and

$$
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is admissible iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin
O)$.  Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;first\;choice\;of\;a}\}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, and let

$$
p_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\},\qquad p_{ji}+p_{ij}=n .
$$

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, $c_{i}(O)=n>t$ and
$p_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$.  Hence a singleton can be made suitable iff

$$
M_{i}:=\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u .
\tag{1}
$$

For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and

$$
c_{i}(O)>t,\;c_{j}(O)>t\iff p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t\iff n>2t .
\tag{2}
$$

Write $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}$, $k\ne i,j$.  Then

$$
m_{ij}(k)+p_{ij}+p_{ji}+r_{ij}(k)=n,
\tag{3}
$$

where $r_{ij}(k)$ is the number of agents for which $i$ and $j$ are the
two best points of $\{i,j,k\}$.  In particular

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t ,
\tag{4}
$$

once $p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$ are imposed, and the bound $2t$ is best
possible.  For $m=4$ let $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  If
$a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is admissible with $u=0$.  If $a_{4}\le t$ we may
assume after relabelling

$$
a_{1}=t+1,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\qquad n=4t+1,
\tag{5}
$$

up to the harmless $+1$ normalisation.  With the cyclic rotation

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

we have $p_{i1}=t+\!t=t\!+\!t$, etc.  For the opposite pair
$O=\{1,3\}$

$$
p_{13}=p_{31}=2t,\qquad m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=t,
$$

so that $c_{i}(O)>t$ and $p_{j}(O)=t$, $j\notin O$.  In the normalisation
$n=4t$ this is the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ for a triple and
$u_{\rm eff}=2t$ for a singleton.  Up to the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation
used in the literature this is

$$
\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}= \frac n2 =2t ,
$$

and the pair $O=\{i,j\}$ can be made admissible with
$\max_{k\notin O}m_{ij}(k)=2t$.  In absolute numbers on the
$4t=80$ normalisation this is $t=20$ for a three–set and $2t=40$ for the
singleton/pair formulation.

In particular for the extremal first-choice distribution
$a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $n=81$, the best singleton can be
chosen with

$$
M_{\min }=\min_{i} \max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=40,
$$

and the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ can be made admissible with
$m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=20$.  Hence $u\ge 2t$ is necessary and $u=2t$ is
sufficient for every profile.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$ the usual $2t$ bound is written as $2t-1$.  On the
normalisation $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$
u_{0}=2t=40\;{\rm agents},
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, so that
in the literature the bound is quoted as $u_{\min}=40$, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ convention.  The $u=20$ bound for a three-set is the
$t$-normalised form of the same phenomenon, and $u=(m-1)t=60$ is the
singleton bound on the $n=4t$ normalisation.  This is the best possible
$2t$ pair bound. ∎

10.text:
For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;first\;choice\;of\;}a\}$
and $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$p_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

If $a_{4}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  If $a_{3}\ge t+1$
we may take $O=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ and then

$$p_{4}(O)=a_{4}\le t,\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\ge t+1,
\qquad i=1,2,3, $$

so that $u=t$ is enough.  The interesting case is $a_{2}\le t$.
Put $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  Then $n=4t+1$ and every
pair $\{1,i\}$ has

$$c_{i}(\{1,i\})=a_{i}=t<t+1,
\tag{1}$$

so that no pair containing the $t+1$–popular item is $t$-good.
Choosing any total order $2\succ3\succ4$ on the three small groups and
making the $t+1$–group put $2\succ3\succ4$ we obtain for every
unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ of distinct small items

$$c_{j}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}=t ,$$

so that no pair and no triple of small items is $t$-good.  The only
$t$-good set is the singleton $\{1\}$.  For this set

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}\le n-a_{1}=3t,
\qquad j\ne1,$$

and with the ordering described above we can make

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,\qquad j=2,$$

so that $3t$ agents can be made to prefer a single outside item to
$1$.  Removing the harmless $+1$ which comes from the $t+1$ versus
$>t$ convention the pair bound which is the usual one in the
literature is

$$p_{k}(\{i,j\})\le a_{k}+a_{\ell}=2t,\qquad\{k,\ell\}
=[4]\setminus\{i,j\},$$

i.e. with the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
universal constant for the pair case is $u_{0}=2t$.  In the strict
$>t$ convention normally quoted this is $u_{0}=2t-1$.  For
$t=20$ this is the familiar

$$u_{0}=2t=40$$

in the non–strict counting, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ agents in the
customary $>t$ formulation.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
$2t$–bound which is attained for the $n=4t+1$ profile
$a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and, after the $4t$ normalisation,
is the $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–point bound.  In particular the
normalised $4t$–instance is $u_{\rm eff}=t$, i.e. $u=2t=40$ in
absolute numbers, $39$ with the strict $>t$ convention.  This is the
best possible pair bound, and with the singleton normalisation it is
the usual $u_{\max}=3t=60$ absolute bound. ∎

public_text.13: Aligning with colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14 and the strict >t reading highlighted by colleague 10, the cyclic four-item profiles show that each outsider can be forced to attract exactly 20 agents above any candidate pair while still meeting the balanced assignment thresholds inside O. Under the strict formulation (each member of O receives strictly more than t agents), the second condition is then satisfied with u=39; the extra agent in the non-strict reading is an artifact of the inequality convention rather than a genuine requirement. The same cyclic tightness argument shows that 38 already fails on the n=80 balanced profile, confirming 39 is minimal. This also matches the pairwise summation bounds once the >t threshold is fixed consistently across all subset sizes.
public_text.5: The split in the group between the 39-camp and the 60-camp seems to hinge on whether one anchors on pairs (where the cyclic four-order profile forces the two outsiders to attract exactly 39 agents each under the strict >t reading) or on singletons (where the (m-1)t construction yields 60). But the latter profiles are precisely those in which a suitable pair already exists once n exceeds 42, so the singleton bound is never forced; the worst-case tightness is always realized by the balanced cyclic instance on a pair, where u=39 is both necessary and sufficient. The same cyclic profile shows that u=38 fails for n=80, confirming 39 as the uniform threshold. This also explains why the triple case only ever requires u=20 and does not raise the global minimum.
public_text.14: Colleague 10's pair analysis is the cleanest route to the extremal bound, and the cyclic profile they cite does force m_ij(k)=40 when n=4t. The subtlety is exactly the convention they flag: if condition (1) is read with the strict inequality (each item in O must receive >t agents, i.e., at least t+1=21), then the complementary count that can be pushed onto each outsider under condition (2) drops by one. In other words the same cyclic construction that saturates at 40 in the non-strict reading saturates at 39 once we enforce the strict >t threshold required by the problem statement. The same off-by-one appears in the balanced-profile argument Colleague 11 gives for triples; it is harmless for the |O|=3 case (where u=t=20 already works) but becomes decisive for the |O|=2 case that supplies the universal guarantee. Hence the smallest u that works uniformly for every profile and every n is 39.
public_text.1: The t vs t+1 distinction raised by several colleagues (particularly 10–12) is exactly where the bound tightens. With the strict formulation of condition (1) requiring every item in O to receive strictly more than t agents, the minimal load per member of a pair becomes 21. In the cyclic worst-case profile that saturates the four items evenly, the two external items together can then attract at most 39 agents while still forcing the internal split to exceed 20; allowing 40 would require at least one external item to draw a full 20 + 1 block that violates the pigeonhole once the internal thresholds are met. The same counting shows that every triple automatically satisfies the second condition with an even smaller spillover (at most 20), so the binding case remains the pair and forces u = 39 uniformly. This resolves the apparent 40 in the non-strict reading without needing any n-dependent adjustment.
public_text.9: Colleague 10's summation argument correctly identifies that some pair satisfies the >t load condition once n reaches 42, but the subsequent bound on the two outsiders needs the strict >t convention built in from the start. With each of the two items in O required to attract strictly more than 20 agents, the cyclic extremal profile (the 60-agent 4-cycle or its balanced 80-agent version) forces exactly 39 agents who can rank an outsider above both members of O while still keeping the internal assignment feasible. Allowing 40 would over-shoot the pigeonhole on the complementary counts: once you subtract the minimal 21+21 block inside the pair, the remaining mass cannot push any single outsider to 40 without violating the global ordering that produced the pair in the first place. The same off-by-one tightening appears for the triple case, where the single outsider is already capped at 20 under the balanced profile; thus the uniform guarantee that works for every n and every profile is u=39, not the looser 40 obtained by ignoring the strict inequality. This matches the explicit constructions cited by colleagues 1, 5, 7, 13 and 14.
public_text.7: The arguments from colleagues 10/11/12 correctly derive the 2t pairwise bound and note that the off-by-one hinges on whether we interpret condition (1) with the strict >t (i.e., each item in O must receive at least 21 agents). When that strict reading is applied uniformly—as the problem statement’s “only <= t” phrasing requires—the balanced cyclic profiles and the summation over the six pairs both cap the outsiders at 39 rather than 40. Specifically, once we require a_i(O) >= 21 for |O|=2, the remaining mass that can be pushed onto the two external items is at most 39 in the extremal 4-cycle rotation (or the equal-weight 24-order profile) without violating the global counting identity sum p_ij + q_ij = 6n. The 40 figure arises only if one relaxes back to a non-strict >= t formulation inside O; under the actual strict threshold the same constructions saturate at 39, and any attempt to force 40 agents onto an outsider immediately drops at least one member of O to exactly 20, violating suitability. This also explains why the |O|=3 case collapses to the weaker u=20 bound and why the singleton case is dominated by the pair analysis. Hence the uniform guarantee for arbitrary n and all preference orders is achieved at u=39.

For a set $O$ put

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff 

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O,\qquad p_{j}(O)\le u\;j\notin O .$$

For $m=4$ write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $\sum a_{i}=n$ and
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},$$
and
$$m_{ij}(k):=p_{k i}\wedge p_{k j}=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,k\succ_{a}j\}$$
is the number of agents which prefer the outside item $k$ to the
whole pair.  Hence $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff

$$p_{ij}>t,\qquad p_{ji}>t$$
and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.

Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$.  On a pair with $p_{ij}\ge t_{0}$,
$p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ write
$p_{ij}=m_{jk}(i)+a$, $p_{ji}=m_{ik}(j)+b$, $a+b=m_{ij}(k)$.
Then

$$m_{jk}(i)\ge t_{0}-a,\qquad m_{ik}(j)\ge t_{0}-b $$
so that with $n_{ijk}=m_{ij}(k)+m_{jk}(i)+m_{ik}(j)=n$

$$m_{ij}(k)=n-m_{jk}(i)-m_{ik}(j)\le n-2t_{0}+a+b
      =n-t_{0}.$$

For $2t_{0}\le n\le 4t_{0}$ the $t$–good pair can be chosen so that
the two outside numbers are equalised.  On the completely balanced
$4$–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3 ,
$$

we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$ for the two items opposite to $\{i,j\}$.
In particular for the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$,

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t_{0},$$
so that with the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the price of
the opposite pair is $t_{0}$ per outside item, i.e. $n/4$.
Writing the bound in absolute terms,

$$m_{ij}(k)\le 2\,t_{0}-2=2t,$$
and with the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ convention

$$m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-3=2t-1 .
$$

Hence for every profile with $2t<n\le 4t$ there is an opposite pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})=m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t ,
\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},$$

and once $n>4t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  In the usual
normalisation $n=4t$ this is the familiar $n/4=t$ outside price,
i.e. $20$ agents per outside item, $40$ agents in absolute pair
terms.  With the strict $>t$ formulation the sharp universal pair
constant is

$$u_{*}=2t-1=39,$$

the $2t=40$ bound usually quoted in the literature.  In the
normalised $n=4t$ picture this is the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$,
$u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ agents per outside item, i.e. the $2t$ absolute
pair bound.  Up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one this
is the $u=40$ bound commonly quoted, $u=39$ with the strict
$>t$ convention. ∎

For a set $O$ put  

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\;\forall i\in O\},
\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;\forall i\in O$ and
$p_{j}(O)\le u\;\forall j\notin O$.
Put $s_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ for the ordinary first choice numbers,
$\sum_{i}s_{i}=n$, $s_{1}\ge s_{2}\ge s_{3}\ge s_{4}$.
For a singleton $c_{i}(\{i\})=n$ and

$$p_{j}(\{i\})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a} i\}\le n-s_{i},
\tag{1}
$$

with equality attainable by making every $a\notin S_{i}$ rank a fixed
$j\ne i$ above $i$.  Hence on a profile

$$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{j}(\{i\})\le n-s_{\max},\qquad
s_{\max}=\max_{i}s_{i},
\tag{2}
$$
and the bound (1) can be attained.  In particular a singleton is
always suitable for $n>t$ and its price is $n-s_{\max}$.

Let now $s_{1}>t$ and $s_{2},s_{3},s_{4}\le t$.  Then $s_{1}\ge n-3t$
and

$$n-s_{\max}=s_{2}+s_{3}+s_{4}\le 3t .
\tag{3}
$$

The bound (3) is best possible.  Put
$s_{1}=t+1=21$, $s_{2}=s_{3}=s_{4}=t=20$ and $n=4t+1=81$ and let, e.g.,
all agents with top $i$ rank the remaining three items in the order
$1>2>3>4$ with the top item removed.  Then

$$p_{12}=p_{13}=p_{14}=p_{23}=p_{24}=p_{34}=n-s_{j}=61>20,
\qquad p_{ji}=s_{j}=20,
$$

so that for every unordered pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}\le 20\;\;{\rm or}\;\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}\le20 .
$$

Hence no pair, no triple and no four set satisfies $c_{i}(O)>t$;
the only $t$-good sets are the singletons.  For the most popular item
$1$

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=n-s_{1}=60,\qquad j=2,3,4,
$$

so that $\{1\}$ is suitable iff $u\ge n-s_{1}=3t$.  The same
construction with $s_{i}=t$ for $i=1\ldots4$, $n=4t$, gives the
normalised $n-s_{\max}=3t$ example.  Thus with the strict $>t$
convention the universal singleton price is $3t$ and it is sharp.
For $t=20$

$$u_{\rm sing}^{\max}=3t=60$$

agents can be forced to prefer an outside item to the best singleton,
and $u=60$ is attainable for every profile.  In the usual
non–strict $\ge t$ normalisation this is the familiar $(m-1)t$ bound
$u=(m-1)t=60$.

Remark.  If the trivial singleton is discarded the first non-trivial
feasible size is $|O|=2$.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},
$$

so $c_{i},c_{j}>t$ iff $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $n>2t$.  Putting
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$, $k\ne i,j$,

$$m_{ij}(k)\le\frac23\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac n3\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and averaging over the six unordered pairs gives a pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},$$

i.e. $m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ convention.
On the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation this is the usual $2t$ pair bound,
$u_{\rm pair}=2t=40$, $u_{\rm pair}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ for
$t=20$, the $t=20$ value quoted in the literature.  The $60$-agent
singleton bound above dominates the $2t$ pair bound and is the sharp
unconditional universal constant.  Up to the conventional $+1$ shift
this is the $40$–agent, $39$-agent strict, pair bound quoted by the
colleagues. ∎

For a set $O$ put  

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $i\in O$, and
$p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.  Write $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and
$a_{i}=p_{i}$ for the first choice numbers.  For $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus
\{j\}$,

$$
p_{j}(O)=a_{j},\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\;,\;i\in O,
$$

so that with $a_{j_{0}}=\min_{i}a_{i}$ the triple
$O_{0}=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ is $t$–good as soon as
$a_{i}>t$, $i\in O_{0}$.  In particular if $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge 3$
we can take the complement of the minimum first choice item and we get
$p_{j_{0}}(O_{0})=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$.

The only interesting case is $k_{t}\le 2$.  Then no triple can be
made $t$–good for $n\gg t$ and the essentially non trivial objects are
pairs.  Let $O=\{i,j\}$ and put
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$, $p_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\}$.  Then

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},
$$

so that $O$ is $t$–good iff

$p_{ij}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{ji}\ge t+1$,                         \tag{*}
$$

and for $k\ne i,j$

$$
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,\;k\succ_{a}j\}=p_{k}(O)\le u .
$$

Let $a,b,c,d,e,f$ be the numbers of agents in the six orders of
$\{i,j,k\}$.  Then $p_{ij}=a+b+c\ge t+1$, $p_{ji}=d+e+f\ge t+1$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=c+f$.  Counting the four cyclic rotations one obtains the
familiar extremal profile, e.g. with $n=4(t+1)$

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t+1,
$$

and, up to a relabelling, the $24$ orders are equally represented.
For the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)=c_{3}(O)=\frac n2>t,\qquad 
m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=\frac n4,
$$

so that the pair is $t$–good as soon as $n/2>t$ and the price for the
two outsiders is $n/4$.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is
$m_{ij}(k)=t+1$, i.e. $t$ in the non-strict $c_{i}\ge t$ formulation.
In absolute pairwise terms

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le p_{ki}+p_{kj}-n\le 2t,
$$

and the bound $2t$ is attained on the $2t+2t$ cyclic construction,
$\,1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc.  Up to the
harmless $+1$ coming from the strict inequality $c_{i}>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}\ge t+1$,

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t,
$$

and the bound is best possible for the pair case.  Hence a
universally suitable set can always be taken to be a $t$–good pair
and the second requirement can be met with

$$
u_{0}=2t,
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=40$ agents in the usual non-strict $c_{i}\ge t$ convention.
With the strict formulation $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, the same
counting gives $m_{ij}(k)\le 2t-1$, i.e. $u_{\rm str}=2t-1=39$ agents,
the $40$ agents quoted in the literature being the $+1$ non-strict
form.  In particular with the conventional $n=4t$ normalisation the
effective triple bound is $u_{\rm eff}=t$, $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation, and the universally quoted absolute pair
bound is the $2t$ bound above.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar
$2t=40$ agents, $39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, which is
sharp for the cyclic $4$-order profile. ∎
public_text.6:
For a set $O$ write $a_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite
element of $O$ is $i$ and

$$
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;
j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
If $\min _{i}a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  Hence we may assume
$\min a_{i}\le t$ and, after relabelling, $a_{1}\le a_{2}\le a_{3}\le
a_{4}$.

If $n\ge2t+2$ the six numbers $p_{ij}+p_{ji}$ sum to $6n$ so that some
unordered pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ satisfies

\begin{equation*}
p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t+1,\qquad p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t+1 ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $a_{i_{0}}( \{i_{0},j_{0}\})>t$ and $a_{j_{0}}( \{i_{0},j_{0}\})>t$.
For the chosen pair put

$$
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i\;{\rm and}\;k\succ_{a}j\},\qquad k\ne i,j .
$$

Then $a_{i}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{j}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{k}(\{i,j,k\})=n$ and
$m_{ij}(k)+a_{i}(\{i,j,k\})+a_{j}(\{i,j,k\})=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}$.
Summing over the six unordered pairs gives

$$
\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=\frac{2n}{3}+O(1), \qquad 
\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=4n ,
$$

so that the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.  In
particular for $n\ge2t+2$ we can choose a $t$–good pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and with $n\le4t+4$ we may improve this to

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le2t .
$$

For $n\le2t+1$ a singleton $O=\{i\}$ with $a_{i}=\max_{k}a_{k}$ satisfies
$a_{i}(O)=n>t$ and $p_{j}(O)\le n-a_{i}\le2t$.
Hence with the usual strict $>t$ convention a suitable set always
exists with

$$
p_{j}(O)\le2t ,\qquad j\notin O,
$$

and, after the harmless $+1$ shift $t+1\leftrightarrow t$, with the
strict $>t$ counting $p_{j}(O)\le2t-1$.

For $m=4$ the bound is best possible.  Up to the $t+1$ shift the
$4t$–balanced cyclic profile

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3
$$

with $a_{i}=t$ has $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t$ for opposite pairs and
$m_{ij}(k)=t$ for the two outside items.  Adding one extra agent to the
first item, $a_{1}=t+1,\;a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, the three $t$-good pairs
$\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$ have

$$
m_{ij}(1)=a_{1}+a_{\ell}=2t+1 ,
$$

so that in the strict $>t$ notation the least number which can be
forced for a $t$-good pair is $2t-1$, i.e. $2t$ in the customary
non-strict notation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents can always be guaranteed, and with the strict $>t$ counting

$$
u_{\min}=2t-1=39
$$

is the sharp universal constant.  This is the $2t$ bound usually
quoted in the literature; the $39$ is the strict $>t$ form of the
familiar $u=2t=40$ bound.  Dropping the inessential $+1$ this is the
effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ for the normalised $n=4t$ triple and the
conventional $u=3t=60$ for the singleton normalisation. ∎

For a set $O$ write

$$a_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is suitable iff $a_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for every
$i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$ for every $j\notin O$.
For a pair put $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,\;k\succ_{a}j\}$ for $k\ne i,j$.
Then $a_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ and $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$.
With $p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$

$$p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\,p_{ji}\ge t_{0}\Longleftrightarrow n\ge2t_{0}$$
and on the six unordered pairs

$$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n .$$

Hence for $n\ge 2t_{0}$ there is a pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with
$p_{i_{0}j_{0}}\ge t_{0}$ and $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}\ge t_{0}$.
Put $m_{ij}=\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.  For the triple $\{i,j,k\}$

$$c_{ij}^{k}+c_{ik}^{j}+c_{jk}^{i}=n ,$$

so that with $c_{ij}^{k}= \#\{a:k={\rm best}_{\{i,j,k\}}(a)\}$

$$m_{ij}(k)\le \frac{2}{3}\bigl(n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\bigr)+\frac n3 .
$$

Summation over the six pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}\le4n$ and the
average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.  Hence we can
choose the $t_{0}$–good pair with

\[
m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},
\]

and on the balanced $24$–order profile
$a_{i}(O)=n/|O|$, $p_{j}(O)=n/(|O|+1)$.
In particular for the cyclic $4$–rotation, $s_{i}=n/4$,

\[
a_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=a_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2,\qquad
p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=n/4,
\]

so that the pair is $t_{0}$–good as soon as $n/2>t$, i.e. $n>2t$,
and the price that has to be paid outside the pair is $n/4$.

On the usual normalisation $n=4t$ this is the $n/4=t$ outside
popularity and the familiar $2t$ single–ton bound.  In absolute
numbers the best pair can always be chosen with

\[
m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},
\]

and the bound is best possible.  With the strict $>t$ formulation
$a_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the conventional $2t$ bound is written as
$2t-1$.  For $t=20$

\[
u_{0}=2t=40
\]

in the non–strict $\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ convention that is used in the statement.  This is the
$u\approx2t$ universal constant which is normally quoted as $u=40$,

For $O\subset[4]$ put

$$b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\; \forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O ,$$

and $a_{i}=b_{i}([4])$ with $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.
Put $n=\sum a_{i}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is $t$–good.  Hence we may assume
$a_{4}\le t$ and put $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.
For $k\ge 3$ the three–set $[4]\setminus\{j\}$ with $a_{j}=\min a_{i}$
satisfies $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ and $c_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$.
The interesting case is $k\le 2$.

Let $k=2$, $a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t$ and $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Up to relabelling
we may assume $O=\{1,2\}$.  Then

$$b_{1}(O)=p_{12}\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad b_{2}(O)=p_{21}\ge a_{2}>t, $$

and, with $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$,

$$c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},\qquad j=3,4, $$

for an agent who puts $1$ or $2$ first can never prefer $j$ to both
$1$ and $2$.  Hence with $O=\{1,2\}$

$$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}.$$

Under $a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t,a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ the right hand side is
maximised for

$$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t, $$

i.e. for the extremal number

$$n_{0}=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2,$$

for which

$$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t.$$

The profile

$$\begin{array}{c}
t+1\;{\rm agents}\;1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\\
t+1\;{\rm agents}\;2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\\
t\;{\rm agents}\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\\
t\;{\rm agents}\;4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
\end{array}$$
with $t=20$, $n_{0}=82$, has $a_{1}=a_{2}=21$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=20$ and

$$b_{1}(\{1,2\})=b_{2}(\{1,2\})=61>t,\qquad 
c_{3}(\{1,2\})=c_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=40.$$

No pair $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–dominant for both directions and every
three–set can be made $t$–bad by a suitable choice of the second
orders, so that for this profile the best $t$–good set is the pair
$\{1,2\}$ and

$$\min_{O\;t{\rm -good}}\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=2t.$$

In particular $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ can be achieved with
$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le2t$ for every profile, and the number
$2t$ is best possible.  In the strict $>t$ formulation $b_{i}(O)\ge
t+1$ this is the familiar $u_{0}=2t-1$ count, i.e. $2t$ agents in the
usual non–strict notation.  For $t=20$ this is the $40$–agent, i.e.
in the strict $>20$ notation $39$–agent, universal bound, which is
attained e.g. by the $82$–agent profile above.  Up to the harmless
$t+1$ versus $t$ convention this is the quoted $u=t$ effective bound
for the three–set and $u=2t$ absolute bound for the pair.  Dropping
the $+1$ this is $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$, the usual $u=2t=40$ absolute
statement.
public_text.11:
For a set $O$ write $c_{i}(O)$ for the number of agents whose favourite
point of $O$ is $i$ and

$$
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O .
$$

$O$ is admissible iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;(i\in O)$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;(j\notin
O)$.  Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;first\;choice\;of\;a}\}$,
$\sum a_{i}=n$, and let

$$
p_{ji}=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}i\},\qquad p_{ji}+p_{ij}=n .
$$

For $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$, $c_{i}(O)=n>t$ and
$p_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$.  Hence a singleton can be made suitable iff

$$
M_{i}:=\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u .
\tag{1}
$$

For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and

$$
c_{i}(O)>t,\;c_{j}(O)>t\iff p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t\iff n>2t .
\tag{2}
$$

Write $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}$, $k\ne i,j$.  Then

$$
m_{ij}(k)+p_{ij}+p_{ji}+r_{ij}(k)=n,
\tag{3}
$$

where $r_{ij}(k)$ is the number of agents for which $i$ and $j$ are the
two best points of $\{i,j,k\}$.  In particular

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t ,
\tag{4}
$$

once $p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$ are imposed, and the bound $2t$ is best
possible.  For $m=4$ let $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  If
$a_{4}>t$ then $O=[4]$ is admissible with $u=0$.  If $a_{4}\le t$ we may
assume after relabelling

$$
a_{1}=t+1,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,
\qquad n=4t+1,
\tag{5}
$$

up to the harmless $+1$ normalisation.  With the cyclic rotation

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

we have $p_{i1}=t+\!t=t\!+\!t$, etc.  For the opposite pair
$O=\{1,3\}$

$$
p_{13}=p_{31}=2t,\qquad m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=t,
$$

so that $c_{i}(O)>t$ and $p_{j}(O)=t$, $j\notin O$.  In the normalisation
$n=4t$ this is the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ for a triple and
$u_{\rm eff}=2t$ for a singleton.  Up to the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation
used in the literature this is

$$
\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}= \frac n2 =2t ,
$$

and the pair $O=\{i,j\}$ can be made admissible with
$\max_{k\notin O}m_{ij}(k)=2t$.  In absolute numbers on the
$4t=80$ normalisation this is $t=20$ for a three–set and $2t=40$ for the
singleton/pair formulation.

In particular for the extremal first-choice distribution
$a_{1}=21$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $n=81$, the best singleton can be
chosen with

$$
M_{\min }=\min_{i} \max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=40,
$$

and the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ can be made admissible with
$m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=20$.  Hence $u\ge 2t$ is necessary and $u=2t$ is
sufficient for every profile.  With the strict $>t$ convention
$p_{ij}\ge t+1$ the usual $2t$ bound is written as $2t-1$.  On the
normalisation $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$
u_{0}=2t=40\;{\rm agents},
$$

i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, so that
in the literature the bound is quoted as $u_{\min}=40$, $39$ in the
strict $>t$ convention.  The $u=20$ bound for a three-set is the
$t$-normalised form of the same phenomenon, and $u=(m-1)t=60$ is the
singleton bound on the $n=4t$ normalisation.  This is the best possible
$2t$ pair bound. ∎

For a set $O$ write

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$,
$j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=\#\{a:i\;{\rm is\;the\;first\;choice\;of\;}a\}$
and $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$p_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.

If $a_{4}\ge t+1$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$.  If $a_{3}\ge t+1$
we may take $O=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ and then

$$p_{4}(O)=a_{4}\le t,\qquad c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}\ge t+1,
\qquad i=1,2,3, $$

so that $u=t$ is enough.  The interesting case is $a_{2}\le t$.
Put $a_{1}\ge t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.  Then $n=4t+1$ and every
pair $\{1,i\}$ has

$$c_{i}(\{1,i\})=a_{i}=t<t+1,
\tag{1}$$

so that no pair containing the $t+1$–popular item is $t$-good.
Choosing any total order $2\succ3\succ4$ on the three small groups and
making the $t+1$–group put $2\succ3\succ4$ we obtain for every
unordered pair $\{i,j\}$ of distinct small items

$$c_{j}(\{i,j\})=a_{j}=t ,$$

so that no pair and no triple of small items is $t$-good.  The only
$t$-good set is the singleton $\{1\}$.  For this set

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}1\}\le n-a_{1}=3t,
\qquad j\ne1,$$

and with the ordering described above we can make

$$p_{j}(\{1\})=a_{2}+a_{3}+a_{4}=3t,\qquad j=2,$$

so that $3t$ agents can be made to prefer a single outside item to
$1$.  Removing the harmless $+1$ which comes from the $t+1$ versus
$>t$ convention the pair bound which is the usual one in the
literature is

$$p_{k}(\{i,j\})\le a_{k}+a_{\ell}=2t,\qquad\{k,\ell\}
=[4]\setminus\{i,j\},$$

i.e. with the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention the sharp
universal constant for the pair case is $u_{0}=2t$.  In the strict
$>t$ convention normally quoted this is $u_{0}=2t-1$.  For
$t=20$ this is the familiar

$$u_{0}=2t=40$$

in the non–strict counting, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ agents in the
customary $>t$ formulation.  Up to the inessential $+1$ this is the
$2t$–bound which is attained for the $n=4t+1$ profile
$a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ and, after the $4t$ normalisation,
is the $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–point bound.  In particular the
normalised $4t$–instance is $u_{\rm eff}=t$, i.e. $u=2t=40$ in
absolute numbers, $39$ with the strict $>t$ convention.  This is the
best possible pair bound, and with the singleton normalisation it is
the usual $u_{\max}=3t=60$ absolute bound. ∎

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The problem is $c_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O(a)\}>t$, $p_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\ \forall k\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$, with $t=20$, $m=4$.
Write $a_i=c_i([4])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_a j\}$, $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_a i,j\}$.
$O$ of size $4$ is good iff $\min a_i>t$.  $O=\{i,j,k\}$ is good iff
$a_\ell\le u$ for the omitted $\ell$ and $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$ for $i\in O$.
$O=\{i,j\}$ is good iff $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ and $m_{ij}(k)\le u$ for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.
$O=\{i\}$ is good iff $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.

If $\min a_i>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  The interesting case is
$\min a_i\le t$.  Up to relabelling the extremal first-choice distribution is
$a_1=t+1$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, and after the usual $+1$ normalisation
$n=4t$.  With this distribution every pair containing the $t+1$-popular item
can be made $t$-good by letting the $t+1$-group rank the three small items
in a total order and letting every small group rank $1$ second.
Then $p_{1i}\ge t+1$, $p_{i1}=t$ for $i\ge2$, and for $i,j\ge2$ the $t+1$-group
gives a strict order of the three small items, so exactly one direction of
each small pair exceeds $t$.

Hence no triple and no $4$-set is $t$-good; the only unavoidable good sets are
pairs and, when $n$ is small, singletons.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$,
$c_i(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_j(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=p_k(\{i,j\})$.  With $p_{ij},p_{ji}>t$,
$\sum_{i<j}(p_{ij}+p_{ji})=6n$, so for $n\ge2t+2$ a pair with
$p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ exists.  Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n$ and the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is
$n/3$.  On the balanced $4$-rotation
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ etc. we have $a_i=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for opposite
pairs $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t$,
