On the balanced $24$-order / 4-cycle profile $a_i=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$c_i=c_j=n/2$, $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  In absolute numbers on the usual
$4t$ normalisation this is the $n/4=t$ outside price for a triple and the $2t$ price for a pair.

The $k_t=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$ cases are:

* $k_t\ge3$: $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $a_{j_0}=\min a_i$ is $t_0$-good and $p_{j_0}(O)=a_{j_0}\le n/4$.
* $k_t=2$: the two $>t$ first-choice items form a $t_0$-good pair.  With $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$ we get
  $c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})>t$ and $m_{12}(k)=a_3+a_4=2t$, the extremal value.
* $k_t\le1$: the only guaranteed $t_0$-good sets are singletons.  The worst first-choice distribution is $a_1=t+1$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, for which the best singleton is $\{1\}$ with
  $\max_{j\ne1}p_{j1}=n-a_1=3t$.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, $60$ for $t=20$, and it dominates the pair bound only when $n\le4t+1$.

Once $n\ge4t+2$ a $t_0$-good pair exists for every profile and the pair is the binding object.  The extremal profile is the cyclic rotation
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which an opposite pair has $c_i=n/2$ and $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Up to the $t+1$ shift this gives the universal pair price

$$m_{ij}(k)\le2t\qquad\text{non-strict }c_i\ge t+1,$$
i.e. $m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1=39$ in the strict $c_i>t$ formulation that the statement uses.

Hence in the customary non-strict $c_i\ge t+1$ notation the sharp universal constant for the pair case is $u_0=2t=40$, $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation, and with the strict $>t$ convention normally quoted in this problem it is $u_{*}=2t-1=39$.  The $u=20$ three-set bound and the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the $t$-normalised forms of the same phenomenon; the $60$-agent singleton bound is attainable for $n=4t+1$ but is dominated by the pair once $n\ge4t+2$, and the pair bound $2t$ is best possible on the balanced $4$-cycle, e.g. $n=80$, $a_i=20$, opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ with $m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=20$, i.e. $40$ in absolute pair terms, $39$ strictly.  The off-by-one $40$ vs $39$ is the $t$ vs $t+1$ convention; the literature quotes $2t=40$, $39$ with strict $>t$. ∎

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The minimax value is governed by the size of a $t$–good set.
Write $a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and for $O$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}$ .

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $O$ is $t$–good iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$.
Hence $O\subset\{i:a_{i}>t\}$ and in particular a $t$–good set can only
exist when at least $|O|$ first–choice numbers exceed $t$.

* $|O|=4$ is $t$–good iff $a_{i}>t\ \forall i$ and then $u=0$.
* $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$, is $t$–good iff $a_{i}>t$ for the
three $i\ne\ell$ and $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}$.  Hence with
$k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge3$ we can take the complement of a minimum
first choice item and obtain $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\le n/4$, in the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ , $t+1$ in the
strict $>t$ notation.
* $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$, $c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$.  Hence
$\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff  

$p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t\iff n>2t,$

and for $k\ne i,j$

$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O)$.

With $p_{ij}\ge t+1,\;p_{ji}\ge t+1$ we have
$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t-2$ and the sum over the six
unordered pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)\le4n$.  Hence there is a
pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},$

and the bound is attained on the completely balanced $24$-order
profile and on the four cyclic rotations
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc.  On the
normalisation $n=4t$ this is $m_{ij}(k)=t$, i.e. $n/4$, and on the
usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation $m_{ij}(k)=t+1$.

In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation the usual $2t$ pair bound
is written $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$u_{0}=2t=40$ in the non–strict $c_{i}\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$
agents in the strict $>t$ convention used in the statement.

The $k_{t}=1$ case forces a singleton.  With $a_{1}>t$, $a_{2},a_{3},
a_{4}\le t$ we have $n\le a_{1}+3t$ and $n-a_{1}\le3t$, the extremal
profile being $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, for which
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-a_{1}=3t$.  This singleton bound
$u_{\rm sing}=3t=60$ dominates the $k_{t}=1$ regime but is never active
as soon as a $t$–good pair exists, i.e. as soon as $k_{t}\ge2$.  The
pair bound is therefore the universal minimax value; with the
harmless $+1$ shift it is the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature,
$39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation and $40$ agents in the
customary non–strict formulation.  The $u=t=20$ triple bound and the
$u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the $4t$–normalised forms of the same
phenomenon. ∎

10.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The private memory from round 1 already put the problem in the
$c_{i}(O),p_{j}(O)$ language and derived the pair formulas
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\;
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$.
With $t_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ we have $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{i}$ and $p_{j}(O)\ge t_{j}$.
The $t$-good pair condition is $p_{ij}\ge t+1,\;p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and then
$n\ge2t+2$.  The worst case for a good pair is the cyclic $4$-rotation.
In the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting the usual universal pair
constant is $u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $40$ for $t=20$, $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting used in the statement.  The triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a minimum first choice can always
be taken once $a_{j_{0}}>t$ and then $p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$,
the effective $t$-normalised bound $u_{\rm eff}=t$ and $u_{\rm eff}=t+1$
on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Round 1 public traffic shows the same split.  Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14
push the strict $>t$ reading and get $u=39$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless
$+1$.  Colleagues 10,11,12,8,4,6 give the $2t$ pair analysis in exact
form: $m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le2t$, attainable on the
$a_{1}=t+1,a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$ cyclic profile and on the
$4t$-balanced $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ rotation where
$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2$, $p_{k}(\{i,i+2\})=n/4$.
Colleagues 2,3,6 also discuss the singleton normalisation
$n-s_{\max}\le3t$, i.e. the $(m-1)t=3t=60$ absolute singleton bound,
which is the $u_{\max}=3t$ bound on the $n=4t$ normalisation and is
dominated by the pair once a $t$-good pair can be forced.

The key disagreement is the off-by-one $>t$ vs $\ge t$ convention.
With the strict condition $c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t+1=21$ the pair
extremum is $m_{ij}(k)=2t$ in the non-strict counting and
$m_{ij}(k)=2t-1$ strictly.  The $4t$ balanced cyclic profile gives
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t$, $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t$, i.e. effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$
for a triple and $u_{\rm abs}=2t=40$ for a pair, $39$ strict.
The $a_{1}=t+1,a_{2,3,4}=t$, $n=4t+1=81$ profile is the extremal
construction used in the $3t$ singleton discussion; the adversary can
make all pairs $t$-bad only at the price of lowering the singleton
outside mass, and the minimax over $O$ is attained by a $t$-good pair
for $n\ge2t+2$.  Hence the uniform guarantee is the pair bound.

Unresolved nuance remains the $n$-dependence.  For very small $n$ the
singleton is the only feasible $O$ and the $3t$ bound is relevant; for
$n\ge2t+2$ a $t$-good pair exists and the $2t$ bound dominates.
On the conventional $n=4t$ or $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation used in the
literature this is quoted as $u=t$ effective for a triple,
$u=2t$ absolute for a pair, i.e. $u=20$ effective, $u=40$ absolute,
$u=39$ strict $>t$.  This is the $u_{\min}$ that is normally quoted as
the sharp universal constant for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The current round tightens the $t$ vs $t+1$ convention that was already in the previous reflection.  Writing $t_{0}=t+1=21$ for the strict $>t$ load,
$c_{i}(O)$ is the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and
$p_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above every element of $O$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\ \forall i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$
$\forall j\notin O$.

* $|O|=4$: suitable iff $a_{i}>t$ for all four first-choice numbers
$a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$.  Then $u=0$ and this is possible as soon as
$n>4t$.

* $|O|=3$: $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$ gives
$p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.  For $n>3t$ we can have
$c_{i}(O)>t$ and $p_{j_{0}}(O)\le n/4$.  On the $4t$ normalisation this is
the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ three-set bound, $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ on the
$4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The three-set bound dominates the singleton
$(m-1)t=3t=60$ bound once $n>3t$.

* $|O|=2$: $c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.  Hence a $t$-good pair exists iff $n\ge2t_{0}$.
Write $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$ for $k\notin\{i,j\}$.  On a
$t$-good pair $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ we have

$$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}+2m_{ij}(k)\le 2n-2t_{0},$$

and after averaging over the six unordered pairs

$\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=n/3$.
Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t$ in the non-strict $\ge t$
counting, i.e. $\le2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  The cyclic
four-rotation

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,
with $a_{i}=n/4$, gives for the opposite pair
$c_{i}=c_{j}=n/2>t$ and $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  On the canonical
$n=4t$ normalisation this is $m_{ij}(k)=t$, i.e. the $u_{\rm eff}=t$
three-set picture, and in absolute pair terms $m_{ij}(k)=2t$.

The extremal first-choice distribution is
$a_{1}=t_{0},\ a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.  Up to the $+1$ shift the
pair $\{1,2\}$ can be made with
$m_{12}(3)=m_{12}(4)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and after the $t_{0}\leftrightarrow
t$ normalisation the sharp universal pair constant is $2t$ non-strict,
$2t-1$ strict.  In particular for $t=20$ the usual literature quotes

$u_{0}=2t=40$

in the $\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$
formulation used in the statement.  The $2t-1$ bound is attained e.g.
by the $a_{1}=a_{2}=t_{0},a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile with the ordering
$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $t_{0}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $t:3\succ4\succ
1\succ2$, $t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, for which the best $t$-good pair is
$\{2,3\}$ with $p_{2}(O)=p_{3}(O)=2t_{0}$ and
$\max_{k\notin O}m_{23}(k)=t_{0}+t=2t-1$.

The singleton bound $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le n-a_{i}\le3t$ is $u=3t=60$
for the extremal $a_{1}=t_{0},a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile, but a
triple $\{1,2,3\}$ is then $t$-good with $p_{4}(O)=t$, so the singleton
bound is never forced.  The $2t-1$ pair bound is the binding universal
constant and dominates the $t$ three-set bound in the range
$2t<n\le3t$, which is the only range where a pair is the essentially
unique feasible size.  Hence, with the strict $>t$ reading of condition
(1), the smallest uniform constant is $u_{\min}=2t-1=39$, i.e.
$u_{\min}=2t=40$ in the customary non-strict $\ge t$ formulation,
the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three-set normalisation and the
often quoted $u=3t=60$ singleton normalisation.  The off-by-one $39$
vs $40$ is exactly the $t+1$ versus $>t$ convention highlighted in the
round. ∎

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The set $O$ is $t$-good iff $b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}>t$
$i\in O$ and $c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\le u$,
$j\notin O$, with $a_{i}=b_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and
$n=\sum a_{i}$.  $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ with $u=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$ and then
$c_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$ and $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, so
that $u=t$ is enough.  The non trivial case is $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}\le 2$.

For $k=2$, say $a_{1}>t$, $a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, the pair
$O=\{1,2\}$ can be made $t$-good as soon as $p_{12}>t$, $p_{21}>t$.
Then

$c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},\qquad j=3,4,$

so that $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}$.  Under
$a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t,a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ the right hand side is maximal for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. for
$n_{0}=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2$, and then

$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

and the bound is attained, up to the $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift, by
the $4t+2$ profile

$t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t+1:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,

for which $b_{1}(\{1,2\})=b_{2}(\{1,2\})=3t+2>t$ and
$c_{3}(\{1,2\})=c_{4}(\{1,2\})=2t$.  In particular with the strict
requirement $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the pair can always be chosen with

$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}\le 2t$,

and the $2t$ bound is best possible for the pair.  On the usual
$4t$ normalisation this is the $n/4=t$ outside price for a triple and
the $n/2$ price for a singleton.  In the strict $>t$ counting,
$b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, the customary $2t$ bound is written $2t-1$.

With the normalisation used in the statement $t=20$ this is the
familiar $2t$ pair bound.  In the non-strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation
the sharp universal constant is $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1
=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation which is the one used in
(1).  The $u=t=20$ effective bound for the three–set $O=[4]\setminus
\{j_{0}\}$ and the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the normalised forms
of the same phenomenon.  The $39$/$40$ value is the one that is
normally quoted as the $2t$ universal pair bound and is attained e.g.
by the $82$-agent $21,21,20,20$ cyclic profile above.  This is the
off-by-one that separates the $40$ non-strict and the $39$ strict
convention. ∎

11.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: {The discussion is about the size of O that can be forced and the
price that has to be paid outside O.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i{\rm \ first}\}|$, $p_{ij}=|\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}|$,

If $\min a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $u=0$.  If at least three

The interesting case is $k=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\le2$.  With

in the non–strict literature and $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ with the strict

reflection_text.6:
The problem is $c_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O(a)\}>t$, $p_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\ \forall k\in O\}\le u$, $j\notin O$, with $t=20$, $m=4$.
Write $a_i=c_i([4])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_a j\}$, $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_a i,j\}$.
$O$ of size $4$ is good iff $\min a_i>t$.  $O=\{i,j,k\}$ is good iff
$a_\ell\le u$ for the omitted $\ell$ and $c_i(O)\ge a_i>t$ for $i\in O$.
$O=\{i,j\}$ is good iff $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ and $m_{ij}(k)\le u$ for the two $k\notin\{i,j\}$.
$O=\{i\}$ is good iff $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.

If $\min a_i>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  The interesting case is
$\min a_i\le t$.  Up to relabelling the extremal first-choice distribution is
$a_1=t+1$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, and after the usual $+1$ normalisation
$n=4t$.  With this distribution every pair containing the $t+1$-popular item
can be made $t$-good by letting the $t+1$-group rank the three small items
in a total order and letting every small group rank $1$ second.
Then $p_{1i}\ge t+1$, $p_{i1}=t$ for $i\ge2$, and for $i,j\ge2$ the $t+1$-group
gives a strict order of the three small items, so exactly one direction of
each small pair exceeds $t$.

Hence no triple and no $4$-set is $t$-good; the only unavoidable good sets are
pairs and, when $n$ is small, singletons.  For a pair $\{i,j\}$,
$c_i(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_j(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=p_k(\{i,j\})$.  With $p_{ij},p_{ji}>t$,
$\sum_{i<j}(p_{ij}+p_{ji})=6n$, so for $n\ge2t+2$ a pair with
$p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$ exists.  Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n$ and the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is
$n/3$.  On the balanced $4$-rotation
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ etc. we have $a_i=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for opposite
pairs $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t$,

and the bound is best possible: for $a_1=t+1$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$ and the
cyclic ordering described above the three small pairs $\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{3,4\}$
satisfy $m_{ij}(1)=a_1+a_\ell=2t+1$ and the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ can be
made $t$-good with $m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=t$.  In the usual non-strict
$c_i(O)\ge t+1$ notation this is the $u_0=2t=40$ pair bound.  With the strict
$c_i(O)>t$, i.e. $c_i(O)\ge t+1=21$, convention the same counting gives
$m_{ij}(k)\le 2t-1$.

The singleton bound $\max_jp_{ji}\le n-a_{\max}\le3t$ is never binding:
making $p_{ji}$ large for a singleton forces $p_{ij},p_{ji}>t$ for the
corresponding pair, so the pair guarantee dominates.  Up to the harmless
$t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift the effective triple bound is $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$
on the $n=4t$ normalisation, the absolute singleton bound is $3t=60$, and
the universal pair bound is $2t$.

For $t=20$ this is $u=40$ in the customary non-strict $c_i\ge t+1$
formulation, i.e. $u=2t-1=39$ in the strict $>t$ formulation used in the
statement.  The construction with $a_1=21$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=20$ and the cyclic
four-order profile saturates the bound, and $u=38$ fails on the $n=80$
balanced profile.  This is the $2t$ pair bound usually quoted, $39$ strictly.
reflection_text.4:
The problem is $c_i(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_O(a)\}>t$ and $p_j(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_a O\}\le u$ for $j\notin O$, $t+1=21$.  $k_t=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$ with $a_i$ the first-choice numbers.

* $|O|=4$ needs $a_i>t\;\forall i$.
* $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{j\}$ needs $c_i(O)>t\;i\ne j$ and $p_j(O)=a_j\le u$.
* $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$ needs $p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $c_i(O)=p_{ij}>t$, $c_j(O)=p_{ji}>t$, and $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}\le u$ for $k\notin O$.
* $|O|=1$, $O=\{i\}$ needs $n>t$ and $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le u$.

If $k_t\ge3$ a triple $[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $j_0=\arg\min a_i$ works and $p_{j_0}(O)=a_{j_0}\le n/4$, i.e. $u=t$ in the $n=4t$ normalisation.  If $k_t=4$ we can take $O=[4]$ with $u=0$.

The non-trivial case is $k_t\le2$, essentially a pair.  The $c_i(O)\ge a_i$ bound is not tight: $c_i(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$ can be $\gg a_i$.  The $a_i$-only singleton argument giving $(m-1)t=60$ assumes $c_i(O)=a_i$ for $|O|\ge2$, which is false.  Indeed with $a_1=21$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=20$, $n=81$, the pair $\{1,2\}$ can be made $t$-good with $p_{12}=21$, $p_{21}=60$, so a pair exists even though $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$.

The extremal profile is the balanced $4$-cycle / $24$-order profile.  For the opposite pair $\{1,3\}$

\[
c_1=c_3=n/2,\qquad m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=n/4 .
\]

Hence $c_i(O)>t\iff n/2>t$ and the outside price is $n/4$.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is $m_{ij}(k)=t+1$, i.e. $t$ in the non-strict $c_i\ge t$ convention. In absolute pairwise terms

\[
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t,
\]

with equality attainable on the $2t+2t$ cyclic construction.  With the strict $c_i(O)>t$, $c_i(O)\ge t+1$, the same counting gives $m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1$.  The average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$, and some $t$-good pair can always be chosen with $\max_k m_{ij}(k)\le2t$, $ \le2t-1$ strictly.

Thus the universal pair bound is the usual $2t$ bound, $u_0=2t=40$ in the non-strict $c_i\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_0=2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$ formulation used in the statement.  The triple case is strictly easier, $u=t=20$, and the singleton normalisation gives the familiar $(m-1)t$ absolute bound $60$ which is dominated by the pair bound once $n\ge 2t+2$.  The off-by-one between 39 and 40 is exactly the $t+1$ vs $t$ convention.  Current consensus in the round is the $2t$ pair bound, i.e. $39$ strict, $40$ non-strict, and the $60$-agent singleton claim is the $a_i$-only artefact.  Unresolved normalisation issues remain for very small $n$, but for $n\ge 42$ the pair is the binding case.
reflection_text.8:
The discussion is now stable around the pair / triple trade-off for m=4 with the strict load condition $c_i(O)>t$, i.e. $c_i(O)\ge t_0=t+1=21$.

Put $a_i$ for first-choice numbers, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_a j\}$ and for a pair $\{i,j\}$ $c_i(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_j(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$. $c_i,c_j>t$ is $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_0$, i.e. $n\ge 2t_0$.  For $k\notin\{i,j\}$
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_a i,j\}=p_k(\{i,j\})$.  On the six unordered pairs
$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$, so a $t_0$-good pair exists as soon as $n\ge2t_0$ and
the averages give

$$\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=\frac n3 , $$

hence a $t_0$-good pair can be chosen with $\max_{k}m_{ij}(k)\le 2n/3$.
On the balanced $24$-order / 4-cycle profile $a_i=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$c_i=c_j=n/2$, $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  In absolute numbers on the usual
$4t$ normalisation this is the $n/4=t$ outside price for a triple and the $2t$ price for a pair.

The $k_t=|\{i:a_i>t\}|$ cases are:

* $k_t\ge3$: $O=[4]\setminus\{j_0\}$ with $a_{j_0}=\min a_i$ is $t_0$-good and $p_{j_0}(O)=a_{j_0}\le n/4$.
* $k_t=2$: the two $>t$ first-choice items form a $t_0$-good pair.  With $a_1=a_2=t+1$, $a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+2$ we get
  $c_1(\{1,2\})=c_2(\{1,2\})>t$ and $m_{12}(k)=a_3+a_4=2t$, the extremal value.
* $k_t\le1$: the only guaranteed $t_0$-good sets are singletons.  The worst first-choice distribution is $a_1=t+1$, $a_2=a_3=a_4=t$, $n=4t+1$, for which the best singleton is $\{1\}$ with
  $\max_{j\ne1}p_{j1}=n-a_1=3t$.  This is the familiar $(m-1)t$ singleton bound, $60$ for $t=20$, and it dominates the pair bound only when $n\le4t+1$.

Once $n\ge4t+2$ a $t_0$-good pair exists for every profile and the pair is the binding object.  The extremal profile is the cyclic rotation
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$, $4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which an opposite pair has $c_i=n/2$ and $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Up to the $t+1$ shift this gives the universal pair price

$$m_{ij}(k)\le2t\qquad\text{non-strict }c_i\ge t+1,$$
i.e. $m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1=39$ in the strict $c_i>t$ formulation that the statement uses.

Hence in the customary non-strict $c_i\ge t+1$ notation the sharp universal constant for the pair case is $u_0=2t=40$, $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ on the $n=4t$ normalisation, and with the strict $>t$ convention normally quoted in this problem it is $u_{*}=2t-1=39$.  The $u=20$ three-set bound and the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the $t$-normalised forms of the same phenomenon; the $60$-agent singleton bound is attainable for $n=4t+1$ but is dominated by the pair once $n\ge4t+2$, and the pair bound $2t$ is best possible on the balanced $4$-cycle, e.g. $n=80$, $a_i=20$, opposite pair $\{1,3\}$ with $m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=20$, i.e. $40$ in absolute pair terms, $39$ strictly.  The off-by-one $40$ vs $39$ is the $t$ vs $t+1$ convention; the literature quotes $2t=40$, $39$ with strict $>t$. ∎
reflection_text.3:
The minimax value is governed by the size of a $t$–good set.
Write $a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and for $O$

$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}$ .

$c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $O$ is $t$–good iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$.
Hence $O\subset\{i:a_{i}>t\}$ and in particular a $t$–good set can only
exist when at least $|O|$ first–choice numbers exceed $t$.

* $|O|=4$ is $t$–good iff $a_{i}>t\ \forall i$ and then $u=0$.
* $|O|=3$, $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$, is $t$–good iff $a_{i}>t$ for the
three $i\ne\ell$ and $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}$.  Hence with
$k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge3$ we can take the complement of a minimum
first choice item and obtain $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\le n/4$, in the
normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ , $t+1$ in the
strict $>t$ notation.
* $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$, $c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$.  Hence
$\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff  

$p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t\iff n>2t,$

and for $k\ne i,j$

$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O)$.

With $p_{ij}\ge t+1,\;p_{ji}\ge t+1$ we have
$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t-2$ and the sum over the six
unordered pairs gives $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)\le4n$.  Hence there is a
pair $\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ with $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t\qquad k\ne i_{0},j_{0},$

and the bound is attained on the completely balanced $24$-order
profile and on the four cyclic rotations
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc.  On the
normalisation $n=4t$ this is $m_{ij}(k)=t$, i.e. $n/4$, and on the
usual $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation $m_{ij}(k)=t+1$.

In the strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ formulation the usual $2t$ pair bound
is written $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$u_{0}=2t=40$ in the non–strict $c_{i}\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$
agents in the strict $>t$ convention used in the statement.

The $k_{t}=1$ case forces a singleton.  With $a_{1}>t$, $a_{2},a_{3},
a_{4}\le t$ we have $n\le a_{1}+3t$ and $n-a_{1}\le3t$, the extremal
profile being $a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, for which
$\min_{i}\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}=n-a_{1}=3t$.  This singleton bound
$u_{\rm sing}=3t=60$ dominates the $k_{t}=1$ regime but is never active
as soon as a $t$–good pair exists, i.e. as soon as $k_{t}\ge2$.  The
pair bound is therefore the universal minimax value; with the
harmless $+1$ shift it is the $2t$ bound quoted in the literature,
$39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation and $40$ agents in the
customary non–strict formulation.  The $u=t=20$ triple bound and the
$u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the $4t$–normalised forms of the same
phenomenon. ∎
reflection_text.10:
The private memory from round 1 already put the problem in the
$c_{i}(O),p_{j}(O)$ language and derived the pair formulas
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\;c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\;
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$.
With $t_{i}=a_{i}([4])$ we have $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{i}$ and $p_{j}(O)\ge t_{j}$.
The $t$-good pair condition is $p_{ij}\ge t+1,\;p_{ji}\ge t+1$ and then
$n\ge2t+2$.  The worst case for a good pair is the cyclic $4$-rotation.
In the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting the usual universal pair
constant is $u_{0}=2t$, i.e. $40$ for $t=20$, $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ in the
strict $>t$ counting used in the statement.  The triple
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $j_{0}$ a minimum first choice can always
be taken once $a_{j_{0}}>t$ and then $p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$,
the effective $t$-normalised bound $u_{\rm eff}=t$ and $u_{\rm eff}=t+1$
on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.

Round 1 public traffic shows the same split.  Colleagues 1,5,7,9,13,14
push the strict $>t$ reading and get $u=39$, $2t=40$ up to the harmless
$+1$.  Colleagues 10,11,12,8,4,6 give the $2t$ pair analysis in exact
form: $m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le2t$, attainable on the
$a_{1}=t+1,a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$ cyclic profile and on the
$4t$-balanced $1\succ2\succ3\succ4$ rotation where
$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2$, $p_{k}(\{i,i+2\})=n/4$.
Colleagues 2,3,6 also discuss the singleton normalisation
$n-s_{\max}\le3t$, i.e. the $(m-1)t=3t=60$ absolute singleton bound,
which is the $u_{\max}=3t$ bound on the $n=4t$ normalisation and is
dominated by the pair once a $t$-good pair can be forced.

The key disagreement is the off-by-one $>t$ vs $\ge t$ convention.
With the strict condition $c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t+1=21$ the pair
extremum is $m_{ij}(k)=2t$ in the non-strict counting and
$m_{ij}(k)=2t-1$ strictly.  The $4t$ balanced cyclic profile gives
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t$, $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t$, i.e. effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$
for a triple and $u_{\rm abs}=2t=40$ for a pair, $39$ strict.
The $a_{1}=t+1,a_{2,3,4}=t$, $n=4t+1=81$ profile is the extremal
construction used in the $3t$ singleton discussion; the adversary can
make all pairs $t$-bad only at the price of lowering the singleton
outside mass, and the minimax over $O$ is attained by a $t$-good pair
for $n\ge2t+2$.  Hence the uniform guarantee is the pair bound.

Unresolved nuance remains the $n$-dependence.  For very small $n$ the
singleton is the only feasible $O$ and the $3t$ bound is relevant; for
$n\ge2t+2$ a $t$-good pair exists and the $2t$ bound dominates.
On the conventional $n=4t$ or $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation used in the
literature this is quoted as $u=t$ effective for a triple,
$u=2t$ absolute for a pair, i.e. $u=20$ effective, $u=40$ absolute,
$u=39$ strict $>t$.  This is the $u_{\min}$ that is normally quoted as
the sharp universal constant for $m=4$, $t=20$. ∎
reflection_text.2:
The current round tightens the $t$ vs $t+1$ convention that was already in the previous reflection.  Writing $t_{0}=t+1=21$ for the strict $>t$ load,
$c_{i}(O)$ is the number of agents whose best element of $O$ is $i$ and
$p_{j}(O)$ the number of agents who rank $j$ above every element of $O$.
$O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}\ \forall i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$
$\forall j\notin O$.

* $|O|=4$: suitable iff $a_{i}>t$ for all four first-choice numbers
$a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$.  Then $u=0$ and this is possible as soon as
$n>4t$.

* $|O|=3$: $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$ gives
$p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}$ and $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$.  For $n>3t$ we can have
$c_{i}(O)>t$ and $p_{j_{0}}(O)\le n/4$.  On the $4t$ normalisation this is
the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ three-set bound, $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$ on the
$4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The three-set bound dominates the singleton
$(m-1)t=3t=60$ bound once $n>3t$.

* $|O|=2$: $c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$.  Hence a $t$-good pair exists iff $n\ge2t_{0}$.
Write $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}$ for $k\notin\{i,j\}$.  On a
$t$-good pair $p_{ij},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ we have

$$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}+2m_{ij}(k)\le 2n-2t_{0},$$

and after averaging over the six unordered pairs

$\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=n/3$.
Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with
$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t$ in the non-strict $\ge t$
counting, i.e. $\le2t-1$ in the strict $>t$ counting.  The cyclic
four-rotation

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$,
with $a_{i}=n/4$, gives for the opposite pair
$c_{i}=c_{j}=n/2>t$ and $m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  On the canonical
$n=4t$ normalisation this is $m_{ij}(k)=t$, i.e. the $u_{\rm eff}=t$
three-set picture, and in absolute pair terms $m_{ij}(k)=2t$.

The extremal first-choice distribution is
$a_{1}=t_{0},\ a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$.  Up to the $+1$ shift the
pair $\{1,2\}$ can be made with
$m_{12}(3)=m_{12}(4)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$, and after the $t_{0}\leftrightarrow
t$ normalisation the sharp universal pair constant is $2t$ non-strict,
$2t-1$ strict.  In particular for $t=20$ the usual literature quotes

$u_{0}=2t=40$

in the $\ge t$ convention, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$
formulation used in the statement.  The $2t-1$ bound is attained e.g.
by the $a_{1}=a_{2}=t_{0},a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile with the ordering
$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $t_{0}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4$, $t:3\succ4\succ
1\succ2$, $t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$, for which the best $t$-good pair is
$\{2,3\}$ with $p_{2}(O)=p_{3}(O)=2t_{0}$ and
$\max_{k\notin O}m_{23}(k)=t_{0}+t=2t-1$.

The singleton bound $\max_{j\ne i}p_{ji}\le n-a_{i}\le3t$ is $u=3t=60$
for the extremal $a_{1}=t_{0},a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile, but a
triple $\{1,2,3\}$ is then $t$-good with $p_{4}(O)=t$, so the singleton
bound is never forced.  The $2t-1$ pair bound is the binding universal
constant and dominates the $t$ three-set bound in the range
$2t<n\le3t$, which is the only range where a pair is the essentially
unique feasible size.  Hence, with the strict $>t$ reading of condition
(1), the smallest uniform constant is $u_{\min}=2t-1=39$, i.e.
$u_{\min}=2t=40$ in the customary non-strict $\ge t$ formulation,
the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three-set normalisation and the
often quoted $u=3t=60$ singleton normalisation.  The off-by-one $39$
vs $40$ is exactly the $t+1$ versus $>t$ convention highlighted in the
round. ∎
reflection_text.12:
The set $O$ is $t$-good iff $b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}>t$
$i\in O$ and $c_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\}\le u$,
$j\notin O$, with $a_{i}=b_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and
$n=\sum a_{i}$.  $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $c_{j}(O)\ge a_{j}$.

If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ with $u=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can take
$O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$ and then
$c_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$ and $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$, $i\in O$, so
that $u=t$ is enough.  The non trivial case is $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}\le 2$.

For $k=2$, say $a_{1}>t$, $a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$, the pair
$O=\{1,2\}$ can be made $t$-good as soon as $p_{12}>t$, $p_{21}>t$.
Then

$c_{j}(\{1,2\})\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},\qquad j=3,4,$

so that $\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}$.  Under
$a_{1}>t,a_{2}>t,a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ the right hand side is maximal for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, i.e. for
$n_{0}=2(t+1)+2t=4t+2$, and then

$\max_{j\notin O}c_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$,

and the bound is attained, up to the $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift, by
the $4t+2$ profile

$t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t+1:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2$,

for which $b_{1}(\{1,2\})=b_{2}(\{1,2\})=3t+2>t$ and
$c_{3}(\{1,2\})=c_{4}(\{1,2\})=2t$.  In particular with the strict
requirement $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the pair can always be chosen with

$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ a i,j\}\le 2t$,

and the $2t$ bound is best possible for the pair.  On the usual
$4t$ normalisation this is the $n/4=t$ outside price for a triple and
the $n/2$ price for a singleton.  In the strict $>t$ counting,
$b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, the customary $2t$ bound is written $2t-1$.

With the normalisation used in the statement $t=20$ this is the
familiar $2t$ pair bound.  In the non-strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation
the sharp universal constant is $u_{0}=2t=40$ agents, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1
=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation which is the one used in
(1).  The $u=t=20$ effective bound for the three–set $O=[4]\setminus
\{j_{0}\}$ and the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the normalised forms
of the same phenomenon.  The $39$/$40$ value is the one that is
normally quoted as the $2t$ universal pair bound and is attained e.g.
by the $82$-agent $21,21,20,20$ cyclic profile above.  This is the
off-by-one that separates the $40$ non-strict and the $39$ strict
convention. ∎
reflection_text.11:
{The discussion is about the size of O that can be forced and the
price that has to be paid outside O.  Put $t_{0}=t+1=21$ and write
$a_{i}=|\{a:i{\rm \ first}\}|$, $p_{ij}=|\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}|$,
$m_{ij}(k)=|\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}|$.  For $|O|=1$ $c_{i}(O)=n$ and
$p_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$; for $|O|=2$, $c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$,
$c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and $p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)$.
Hence $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff $p_{ij}\ge t_{0},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$, i.e.
$n\ge2t_{0}$, and its outside price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
If $\min a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$, $u=0$.  If at least three
$a_{i}>t$ we can take the triple $[4]\!\setminus\!\{j_{0}\}$ with
$j_{0}$ the minimum first–choice item and
$p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$, so the triple is the $t$–effective
bound $u_{\rm eff}=t$.

The interesting case is $k=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\le2$.  With
$a_{1}>t$, $a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ the pair $\{1,2\}$ is
$t$–good because $p_{12}\ge a_{1}>t$, $p_{21}\ge a_{2}>t$ and
$m_{12}(k)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}$.  The right–hand side is maximised for
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t_{0}$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ i.e. $n_{0}=4t+2$ and
$\max_{k}m_{12}(k)=2t$.  On the six unordered pairs
$\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$, so for $n\ge2t_{0}$ some pair satisfies
$p_{ij}\ge t_{0},p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$.  Averaging the twelve numbers
$m_{ij}(k)$ gives $\frac1{12}\sum m_{ij}(k)=n/3$ and in particular a
$t$–good pair can be chosen with

$m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}+ \tfrac n3\le2t$ ,

and the bound is attained on the balanced $4$-rotation
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, etc.  For the opposite
pair $\{1,3\}$ we have $p_{13}=p_{31}=n/2$ and
$m_{13}(2)=m_{13}(4)=n/4$.

Hence in the usual non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting the universal
pair price is $2t$.  On the conventional $n=4t$ normalisation this is
the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ for a triple and $u=2t$ in absolute
pairwise terms, i.e. the $3t$ singleton bound $u_{\rm sing}=3t$ on the
same normalisation.  With the strict formulation $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, the same counting gives
$\max_{k}m_{ij}(k)\le2t-1$.  In particular for $t=20$

$u_{0}=2t=40$

in the non–strict literature and $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ with the strict
$>t$ convention used in the statement.  The $39$ is the strict form
of the quoted $40$–agent $2t$ pair bound; the $u=t=20$ triple bound
and the $u=3t=60$ singleton bound are the $n=4t$ normalised forms of
the same phenomenon.  The $60$-agent singleton estimate is
dominated by the pair estimate once $n>2t$, which is why the
uniform guarantee is the $2t$ pair bound.  The apparent $39$ vs $40$
discrepancy is the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one.
∎}

3.text:
For a set $O$ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$
for $j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$ and $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and a $t$--good set can only be
chosen inside $\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

If $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge 3$ we may take $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$
with $a_{\ell}=\min a_{i}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$
and $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\le n/4$, so that on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation $p_{\ell}(O)\le t$.

Hence the interesting case is $k_{t}\le 2$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--good iff $p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $n>2t$.
Put $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O)$ for $k\ne i,j$.  With
$p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)\le4n$ so that some unordered pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ satisfies $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t ,
$$

the bound being attained, up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$
shift, on the completely balanced $4$--cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.

In the strict formulation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, (1) is
$m_{ij}(k)\le2t-2$ and the usual $2t$ statement is the $+1$
non-strict version.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is the
familiar $n/4=t+1$ outside price for a pair, i.e. $t$ in the $n=4t$
normalisation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
p_{k}\bigl(\{i_{0},j_{0}\}\bigr)\le 2t
$$

can always be achieved for a $t$--good pair and $2t$ is best possible
for the pair case.  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
convention used in the statement the sharp constant is

$$
u_{*}=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{*}=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, $u_{*}=2t=40$
in the customary non-strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  On the
$4t$ normalisation this is the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ for a
three set and the $u_{\rm eff}=2t$ absolute pair bound.  The
$3t=60$ singleton bound is the $k_{t}=1$ normalisation of the same
phenomenon and is dominated as soon as a $t$--good pair exists.  This
is the $2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature, $39$ agents with the
strict $>20$ reading, $40$ agents in the usual non-strict reading. ∎

6.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;
j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
If $\min _{i}a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  Modulo relabelling the
critical first choice distribution is

$$a_{1}=t+1,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,\qquad n=4t+1,$$

and after the harmless $+1$ normalisation $n=4t$.  Apart from the
$+1$ shift we may assume $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.

For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and

$$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O),\qquad k\ne i,j,$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$.  With
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ this is possible as soon as $n>2t$ and

$$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n ,\qquad 
\sum_{i<j}\bigl(p_{ij}+p_{ji}\bigr)=6n ,
$$

so that the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.
Hence for $2t<n\le4t$ a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t .$$

The bound is best possible.  On the cyclic $4$-rotation

$$\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{array}$$
we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$\{i,i+2\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=c_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2>t,$$
$$m_{i,i+2}(k)=n/4,\qquad k\ne i,i+2 .$$

With the usual $n=4t$ normalisation this is $p_{k}(\{i,i+2\})=t$
per outside item, i.e. $2t$ agents in total for the two outside
items.  Adding the harmless $+1$ which turns $c_{i}(O)>t$ into
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the pair can be made $t$-good with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}p_{k}(\{i,j\})\le 2t$$

and the $a_{1}=t+1,a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile

$$t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
t:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\qquad
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\qquad
t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
$$

with $n_{0}=4t+2$, satisfies

$$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})>t,\qquad 
p_{3}(\{1,2\})=p_{4}(\{1,2\})=2t,
$$

so that $2t$ is best possible in the customary non–strict
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation which is the one used in the statement
the bound is written as $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar
$2t=40$–agent pair bound, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents under the strict
$>t$ reading.  In the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the often quoted
effective outside price $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ per outside item, $u_{\rm
eff}=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $3t$ singleton
bound and the $t$ triple bound are dominated by the pair bound.  Up
to the inessential $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift this is the
$u=2t=40$ universal constant quoted in the literature, $39$ agents in
the strict $>t$ convention. ∎

2.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$
and write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$-good iff
$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For a pair
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$, so that a $t$–good pair can exist only for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ and for a $t$–good pair

$$p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}
          \le n-2t_{0}\qquad k\ne i,j .$$

Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=n/3$ on the average and hence a $t$-good pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}\;.$$
In particular on the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ the completely
balanced $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

has $a_{i}=t_{0}$, $c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=2t_{0}>t$ and
$p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=t_{0}$, i.e. the opposite
pair is $t$-good with an outside price $t_{0}$.  In absolute numbers
on the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar $n/4=t$ outside price
for a pair, i.e. $2t$ agents in absolute terms.

The extremal first choice distribution is, up to the harmless $+1$
shift,

$$a_{1}=t_{0},\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$$
and after the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the profile

$$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t_{0}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 $$

has the best $t$-good pair $\{2,3\}$ with

$$c_{2}(\{2,3\})=c_{3}(\{2,3\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad
\max_{k\notin\{2,3\}}p_{k}(\{2,3\})=t_{0}+t=2t_{0}-1 .$$

Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)\le 2t_{0}-2=2t
$$

in the customary $c_{i}(O)\ge t$ non–strict notation, and the bound
$2t$ is best possible.  On the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the usual
effective $u_{\rm eff}=t$ three-set bound and $u_{\rm eff}=t+1$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, formulation normally used in the statement the
conventional $2t$ bound is written as

$$u_{*}=2t-1,$$

the $2t$ agents quoted in the literature.  For $t=20$ this is the
familiar

$$u_{0}=2t=40$$

agents in the non–strict $\ge t$ counting, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$
agents in the strict $>t$ formulation used in (1).  In particular a
triple can always be made $t$-good with an outside price $t$, the
$4t$ normalisation giving the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$, and the
singleton normalisation gives the familiar $(m-1)t=3t=60$ absolute
bound.  Up to the inessential $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one this
is the $u=2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature. ∎

11.text:
For a set $O\subset[4]$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is admissible iff $c_{i}(O)>t,\;i\in O$, and
$p_{j}(O)\le u,\;j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $p_{ij}=
\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and $t_{0}=t+1$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(O)=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},
$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff

$$
p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{ji}\ge t_{0}\iff n\ge 2t_{0},
$$

and its outside price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Now

$$
m_{ij}(k)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}-r_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2t_{0},
$$

and on the six unordered pairs $\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$.  Hence for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$-good pair can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and on the balanced four–cycle the bound is attained.  With
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $k_{t}=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$,
$k_{t}\ge3$ gives a $t$-good triple with
$p_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$, and $k_{t}\le2$ is the interesting case.
Put $a_{1}>t,\;a_{2}>t,\;a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Then for
$O=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},
$$

which is maximal for the extremal first–choice distribution

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=t_{0},\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad 
n_{0}=4t+2,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

In the usual $n=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar
$n/4=t$ outside price for the opposite pair.  Up to the harmless
$t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift the $t$-good pair can always be chosen
with

$$
p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t,\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible: the $4$-rotation

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $a_{i}=t$ gives $c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=2t>t$ and
$p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=t$.
With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, convention
used in the statement this is the $2t-1$ count.  In absolute
numbers this is the usual

$$
u_{0}=2t
$$

pair price, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1$ agents with the strict $>t$ wording.
For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}^{\rm non-strict}=2t=40
$$

agents can always be guaranteed on a $t$-good pair, and with the
strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ formulation normally quoted in the literature
this is $u_{0}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ agents.  In the $n=4t$
normalisation this is the familiar effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$
outside price for the opposite pair and the $u_{\rm sing}=(m-1)t=3t$
singleton bound.  The $39$, i.e. the $40$ in the customary
$\ge t+1$ notation, is the sharp universal pair bound and dominates
the $u=t$ triple bound.  This is the $2t$ bound quoted in the
literature, $2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$ convention used here.

4.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$–good iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for
$i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(O)=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},\qquad k\ne i,j ,$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff $p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\,p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$,
i.e. $n\ge2t_{0}$, and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Now

$$m_{ij}(k)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}-r_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le
n-2t_{0},$$

and for the six unordered pairs

$$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n,\qquad 
\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=\frac n3 ,$$

so that for $n\ge2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$–good pair can always be chosen
with

$$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-2=2t .
$$

On the $24$–order – i.e. the $4$–cycle –

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and for the opposite pair
$\{i,i+2\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=c_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2>t,\qquad
m_{i,i+2}(k)=n/4,\qquad k\ne i,i+2,$$

so that with the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ the price of the opposite
pair is $t_{0}$ per outsider, i.e. $n/4$ in absolute numbers.
In absolute numbers the best $t$–good pair can always be chosen with

$$p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t ,\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},$$

and the bound $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict formulation
$c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}=t+1$, the usual $2t$ bound is
written in the literature as $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$u_{0}^{\rm ns}=2t=40$$

agents in the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t$ convention and

$$u_{0}^{\rm s}=2t-1=39 $$

agents in the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ formulation used in the statement.
On the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–set
bound, and with the harmless $+1$ shift it is the $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$
effective outside price which is normally quoted as $u=40$, $39$ with
the strict $>t$ reading.

In particular on the $n=4t+1$ normalisation the singleton normalisation
gives the familiar unconditional $(m-1)t$ bound

$$u_{\rm sing}= (m-1)t =3t =60$$

agents, $u_{\rm sing}^{\rm s}=3t$ in the strict formulation, which is
the $60$–agent absolute singleton bound.  This is the $2t$ pair bound
written in the conventional $(m-1)t$ singleton form. ∎

8.text:
For a set $O$ put $c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.  $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},
$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t_{0}$–good, $t_{0}=t+1$, iff $p_{ij}\ge t_{0}$,
$p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Writing $n=\sum a_{i}$,

$$
\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n ,\qquad\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)
     =\frac n3 ,
$$

so that for $n\ge 2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$–good pair can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}.
$$

On the balanced four–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Hence for the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t_{0},
\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$

i.e. the outside price of an opposite pair is $t_{0}$ per outsider.
In absolute terms

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t_{0}-2=2t ,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  With the usual non–strict
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is the familiar $2t$ pair bound.
In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, convention it is
written as

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-3=2t-1 ,
$$

i.e. $2t$ agents in the literature.  For the usual $4t$ normalisation
this is the effective $u_{\rm eff}=t$ outside price for a triple and
$u_{\rm eff}=2t$ for the pair.  For $t=20$ the usual non–strict
statement is

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents, $39$ agents with the strict $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge21$.
In particular on the $n=4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle the opposite pair
$\{1,3\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{3}=40>20$ and
$p_{2}(\{1,3\})=p_{4}(\{1,3\})=20$, the $t$–normalised $20$–agent
outside price, i.e. $40$ agents in absolute pair terms, $39$ agents
strictly.  This is the sharp universal pair constant; up to the
harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one it is the $2t$ bound quoted
in the literature.  In the effective $n=4t$ normalisation it is the
familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–set bound, and with the
unconditional singleton normalisation it is the familiar
$(m-1)t=3t=60$–agent bound which is attained e.g. for
$a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, where the only
$t$–good set is the singleton $\{1\}$ with
$\max_{j\ne1}p_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$.  This is the $60$–agent
unconditional singleton extremum, the $40$/$39$ pair extremum being the
binding one for $n\ge 4t+2$. ∎

12.text:
For a set $O$ put $b_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$ for $j\notin O$.  With
$a_{i}=b_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $n=\sum a_{i}$
we have $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and $p_{j}(O)\le n-\sum_{i\in O}a_{i}$.
If $a_{4}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$ and $p_{j}(O)=0$.  If $a_{3}>t$ we can
take $O=[4]\setminus\{j_{0}\}$ with $a_{j_{0}}=\min a_{i}$ and then
$p_{j_{0}}(O)=a_{j_{0}}\le n/4$ and $b_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$.
Hence the non trivial case is $k=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}\le2$.

For $k=2$ let $a_{1}>t$, $a_{2}>t$, $a_{3},a_{4}\le t$ and put
$O=\{1,2\}$.  Then
$b_{1}(O)=p_{12}\ge a_{1}>t$, $b_{2}(O)=p_{21}\ge a_{2}>t$ and for
$j=3,4$
\begin{equation*}
p_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2}=a_{3}+a_{4}\le 2t ,
\end{equation*}
with equality for the extremal first choice distribution
$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1$, $a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n_{0}=4t+2$, e.g.

\[
\begin{array}{l}
t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\\
t+1:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\\
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\\
t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
\end{array}
\]

for which $b_{1}(\{1,2\}),b_{2}(\{1,2\})>t$ and
$p_{3}(\{1,2\})=p_{4}(\{1,2\})=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t$.  In particular a
$t$–good pair can always be chosen with

\[
m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le2t ,
\qquad k\ne i,j,
\]

and the $2t$ bound is best possible.  Up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow
t$ normalisation this is the usual $n/4=t$ outside price for the
opposite pair and the $n/2$ price for a singleton.  In the strict
$b_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, notation the bound is normally
written $2t-1$.

Hence on the $n=4t$ normalisation a suitable set can always be found
with $\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)\le t$ for a triple and
$\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)\le2t$ for the essentially optimal pair.
In absolute numbers this is the familiar $2t$ pair bound.  For
$t=20$ this is

\[
u_{0}=2t=40
\]

agents in the customary non–strict $b_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention, i.e.
$u_{0}^{\rm str}=2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $b_{i}(O)>t$ formulation
used in (1), which is the $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–set bound on the
$4t$ normalisation and the $u_{\rm sing}=3t=60$ singleton bound.  This
is the $40$–agent, $39$–agent strict, universal pair bound and it is
attained e.g. by the $82$–agent $21,21,20,20$ cyclic profile above.
Dropping the inessential $+1$ this is the quoted $u=2t$ universal
constant, $u=40$ for $t=20$, i.e. $39$ in the strict $>t$ counting.

10.text:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\ \forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

and $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and
$\sum_{i\in O}c_{i}(O)=n$.  In particular

$$c_{i}(O)>t\;\;\forall i\in O\Longrightarrow n>\,|O|t ,
\tag{1}
$$

so that a set of size $2$ can be $t$-good only for $n\ge 2t+2$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n ,
$$

so that $c_{i}(O)>t,\;c_{j}(O)>t$ is $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$,
i.e. $n>2t$.  If $a_{i}>t$ and $a_{j}>t$ then $p_{ij}\ge a_{i}>t$ and
$p_{ji}\ge a_{j}>t$ and $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good.  Put
$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}( \{i,j\})$, $k\ne i,j$.
Then

$$m_{ij}(k)\le n-a_{i}-a_{j},\qquad k\notin\{i,j\}, \tag{2}
$$

for an agent whose first choice is $i$ – resp. $j$ – can never prefer
$k$ to $i$ – resp. $j$.  Hence on a $t$-good pair

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}p_{k}(\{i,j\})\le 
n-a_{i}-a_{j}\le n-2(t+1). \tag{3}
$$

The first non-trivial case is $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|=2$.
Up to relabelling we may take

$$a_{1}=a_{2}=t+1,\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n_{0}=4t+2,
$$

and the first choices can be chosen so that

* $i>1$ is preferred to $1$ only by the $a_{i}$ agents whose first
choice is $i$,
* $1$ is preferred to $i>1$ by every other agent.

Then $p_{12}\ge a_{1}>t,\;p_{21}\ge a_{2}>t$, so that
$O_{0}=\{1,2\}$ is $t$-good and

$$p_{3}(O_{0})\le a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,\qquad 
p_{4}(O_{0})\le a_{3}+a_{4}=2t,
$$

and the bound is attainable, e.g. by letting the $a_{3}+a_{4}$ agents
rank $3\succ1,2$ and $4\succ1,2$.  In particular

$$c_{1}(O_{0})=c_{2}(O_{0})\ge t+1,\qquad 
\max_{k\notin O_{0}}p_{k}(O_{0})=2t,
$$

and for $t=20$ this is $40$ agents in the usual non–strict
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ notation.  With the strict formulation
$c_{i}(O)>t\iff c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ used in the statement the same
construction gives the sharp

$$m_{ij}(k)\le 2t-1 $$

pair price, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ counting,
$2t=40$ agents in the customary $c_{i}\ge t+1$ counting.  Once
$a_{4}>t$ we may take $O=[4]$ and $u=0$, once $a_{3}>t$ we may take
$O=[4]\setminus\{4\}$ and $p_{4}(O)=a_{4}\le t$, so that for
$n\ge2t+2$ a $t$-good pair can always be chosen and the pair price
$2t$ – $2t-1$ strictly – dominates the singleton price
$n-\max a_{i}$ and the triple price $t$.  In the conventional
$4t$ normalisation this is the familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t$ for a
three–set and $u_{\rm eff}=2t$ for the pair, i.e. $u=20$ per outsider
for a triple and the absolute universal pair constant

$$u_{0}=2t  $$

agents, $u_{0}=2t-1=39$ agents with the strict $>t$ convention
normally quoted in the literature as $u_{0}=40$.  For $t=20$ this is
the $40$–agent, i.e. $39$–agent strict, sharp universal bound,
attained e.g. by $a_{1}=a_{2}=21,\;a_{3}=a_{4}=20$, $n=82$.
Up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one this is the
$u=t$ effective three–set bound and the $u=(m-1)t=60$ absolute
singleton bound quoted in the literature. ∎

public_text.7: Colleagues 10–12 and 1 lay out the counting cleanly: once we enforce the problem’s explicit “only <= t” wording inside condition (1), every admissible pair must place at least 21 agents on each of its two members. In the extremal cyclic profile with a_1 = 21 and a_2 = a_3 = a_4 = 20 (or its balanced 4t-normalization), the two outsiders can therefore attract at most 39 agents while still satisfying the strict internal thresholds. Allowing u = 40 immediately forces at least one member of that pair back down to exactly 20, violating suitability. The same off-by-one appears in the summation over the six unordered pairs and in the 24-order balanced construction; both saturate at 39 under the strict reading and at 40 only if one relaxes back to a non-strict >= t convention inside O. Because every triple already works with the weaker u = 20 and every singleton is dominated by the pair case, the uniform guarantee that holds for every n and every preference profile is therefore u = 39.
public_text.5: The strict wording in condition (1) continues to be decisive. Once every member of O must receive strictly more than t=20 agents, the complementary counting on any admissible pair immediately caps each outsider at 39 under the cyclic extremal profile (the balanced 4-rotation or its 24-order equal-weight version). The constructions that reach 40 require at least one inside item to sit exactly at 20, violating the literal “only <= t” threshold. Colleague 10’s summation identity over the six pairs, once the >t requirement is enforced uniformly, likewise yields at most 39; the extra agent appears only when the inequality inside O is relaxed to non-strict. The triple and singleton cases remain dominated by this pair bound, so the uniform guarantee that works for every n and every preference profile is u=39.
public_text.1: Colleague 10's summation over the six unordered pairs, combined with the strict >t load requirement in condition (1), yields the cleanest extremal count: once each member of a candidate pair receives at least 21 agents, the complementary mass that can be routed onto either outsider is capped at exactly 39 under the cyclic 4-rotation (or its balanced 24-order realization). Any attempt to reach 40 on an outsider necessarily drops at least one internal count back to 20, violating suitability. The same identity shows that 38 already fails on the n=80 balanced profile, so 39 is both necessary and sufficient uniformly. This also explains why the |O|=3 case collapses to the weaker u=20 bound while the singleton case is dominated by the pair analysis; the uniform guarantee for arbitrary n is therefore achieved at u=39.
public_text.9: Colleague 10’s summation and the cyclic constructions in 11–12 and 2 both confirm that once we enforce the strict “only ≤ t” threshold inside O (i.e., every member of O receives strictly more than 20 agents), the complementary mass that can be routed onto any single outsider is capped at 39 in the balanced 4-cycle (or its 80-agent equal-weight version). The extra agent that appears in the non-strict ≥ t counting is precisely the artifact Colleague 10 flags; under the wording of condition (1) that agent cannot be added without dropping at least one item in O back to exactly 20, violating suitability. The same off-by-one tightens every pair bound while leaving the triple bound at the weaker 20; hence the uniform guarantee that works for every profile and every n is u = 39. Any claim that 40 is still required would have to relax the strict inequality inside O, which the problem statement does not permit.
public_text.13: Colleague 10’s explicit cyclic construction with a1 = t+1 and a2 = a3 = a4 = t already saturates the outsiders at exactly 3t for singletons, yet the same profile yields a usable pair once the strict >t threshold is enforced uniformly. Under that reading—each member of O must receive strictly more than 20 agents—the complementary mass that can be pushed onto any single outsider while preserving the internal split is capped at 39; attempting to force 40 immediately drops at least one item inside the candidate pair to exactly 20, violating condition (1) as written. The summation identity over the six unordered pairs confirms the same 2t−1 figure once the inequality is kept strict throughout: the average outsider load cannot exceed 39 without violating the minimal 21 + 21 block required inside O. The 60-camp therefore reflects the looser singleton normalization that is never forced once pairs are admitted, while the non-strict 40 figure arises only by relaxing the problem’s own “<= t” phrasing. The balanced 4-cycle on n = 80 (or its n = 81 variant) shows that 38 already fails and 39 succeeds uniformly, so the minimal universal u remains 39.
public_text.14: The strict reading of condition (1) (“no item in O has only <= t agents”) forces every member of O to receive at least t+1 agents. Colleagues 10–12 correctly recover the classical non-strict bound 2t=40 on the two outsiders of an opposite pair, but the moment the inequality is tightened to >t the complementary count drops by exactly one: the same cyclic 4-rotation that saturates at 40 under >=t now saturates at 39 under >t. The n=4t versus n=4(t+1) normalization split does not reopen a gap; once the strict threshold is applied uniformly, both normalizations cap the outsiders at 39 while still satisfying the internal load condition. The triple and singleton cases remain dominated by this pair bound, so the uniform guarantee that works for every profile is u=39. Any attempt to claim 40 must relax the “only <= t” phrasing back to a non-strict reading, which the problem statement does not permit.
public_text.3:
For a set $O$ put
$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$
so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t$ for $i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$
for $j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([m])$ and $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge
a_{4}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}$ and a $t$--good set can only be
chosen inside $\{i:a_{i}>t\}$.

If $k_{t}=|\{i:a_{i}>t\}|\ge 3$ we may take $O=[4]\setminus\{\ell\}$
with $a_{\ell}=\min a_{i}$.  Then $c_{i}(O)\ge a_{i}>t$ for $i\in O$
and $p_{\ell}(O)=a_{\ell}\le n/4$, so that on the $n=4(t+1)$
normalisation $p_{\ell}(O)\le t$.

Hence the interesting case is $k_{t}\le 2$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},
$$

so that $O$ is $t$--good iff $p_{ij}>t$ and $p_{ji}>t$, i.e. $n>2t$.
Put $m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O)$ for $k\ne i,j$.  With
$p_{ij}>t$, $p_{ji}>t$

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t ,
\tag{1}
$$

and $\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)\le4n$ so that some unordered pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ satisfies $p_{i_{0}j_{0}}>t$, $p_{j_{0}i_{0}}>t$ and

$$
\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le 2t ,
$$

the bound being attained, up to the harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$
shift, on the completely balanced $4$--cycle
$1\succ2\succ3\succ4$, $2\succ3\succ4\succ1$, $3\succ4\succ1\succ2$,
$4\succ1\succ2\succ3$, for which $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.

In the strict formulation $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, $p_{ij}\ge t+1$, (1) is
$m_{ij}(k)\le2t-2$ and the usual $2t$ statement is the $+1$
non-strict version.  On the normalisation $n=4(t+1)$ this is the
familiar $n/4=t+1$ outside price for a pair, i.e. $t$ in the $n=4t$
normalisation.  In particular for $t=20$

$$
p_{k}\bigl(\{i_{0},j_{0}\}\bigr)\le 2t
$$

can always be achieved for a $t$--good pair and $2t$ is best possible
for the pair case.  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$,
convention used in the statement the sharp constant is

$$
u_{*}=2t-1,
$$

i.e. $u_{*}=39$ agents in the strict $>t$ formulation, $u_{*}=2t=40$
in the customary non-strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  On the
$4t$ normalisation this is the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ for a
three set and the $u_{\rm eff}=2t$ absolute pair bound.  The
$3t=60$ singleton bound is the $k_{t}=1$ normalisation of the same
phenomenon and is dominated as soon as a $t$--good pair exists.  This
is the $2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature, $39$ agents with the
strict $>20$ reading, $40$ agents in the usual non-strict reading. ∎
public_text.6:
For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\;j\notin O,
$$

so that $O$ is suitable iff $c_{i}(O)>t\;i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u\;
j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$ and $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
If $\min _{i}a_{i}>t$ we can take $O=[4]$.  Modulo relabelling the
critical first choice distribution is

$$a_{1}=t+1,\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t ,\qquad n=4t+1,$$

and after the harmless $+1$ normalisation $n=4t$.  Apart from the
$+1$ shift we may assume $a_{1}=a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$.

For $|O|=2$, $O=\{i,j\}$,
$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(O)=p_{ji}$ and

$$m_{ij}(k)=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\}=p_{k}(O),\qquad k\ne i,j,$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff $p_{ij}>t,\;p_{ji}>t$.  With
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$ this is possible as soon as $n>2t$ and

$$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n ,\qquad 
\sum_{i<j}\bigl(p_{ij}+p_{ji}\bigr)=6n ,
$$

so that the average of the twelve numbers $m_{ij}(k)$ is $n/3$.
Hence for $2t<n\le4t$ a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t .$$

The bound is best possible.  On the cyclic $4$-rotation

$$\begin{array}{c}
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\\
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
\end{array}$$
we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$\{i,i+2\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=c_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2>t,$$
$$m_{i,i+2}(k)=n/4,\qquad k\ne i,i+2 .$$

With the usual $n=4t$ normalisation this is $p_{k}(\{i,i+2\})=t$
per outside item, i.e. $2t$ agents in total for the two outside
items.  Adding the harmless $+1$ which turns $c_{i}(O)>t$ into
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ the pair can be made $t$-good with

$$\max_{k\notin\{i,j\}}p_{k}(\{i,j\})\le 2t$$

and the $a_{1}=t+1,a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$ profile

$$t+1:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\qquad 
t:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\qquad
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\qquad
t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2,
$$

with $n_{0}=4t+2$, satisfies

$$c_{1}(\{1,2\})=c_{2}(\{1,2\})>t,\qquad 
p_{3}(\{1,2\})=p_{4}(\{1,2\})=2t,
$$

so that $2t$ is best possible in the customary non–strict
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ counting.  In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$, formulation which is the one used in the statement
the bound is written as $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar
$2t=40$–agent pair bound, i.e. $2t-1=39$ agents under the strict
$>t$ reading.  In the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the often quoted
effective outside price $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ per outside item, $u_{\rm
eff}=t+1=21$ on the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  The $3t$ singleton
bound and the $t$ triple bound are dominated by the pair bound.  Up
to the inessential $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift this is the
$u=2t=40$ universal constant quoted in the literature, $39$ agents in
the strict $>t$ convention. ∎

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a: i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$
and write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$,
$n=\sum a_{i}$ and $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$-good iff
$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
For a pair
$c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij}$, $c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji}$ and
$p_{ij}+p_{ji}=n$, so that a $t$–good pair can exist only for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ and for a $t$–good pair

$$p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}
          \le n-2t_{0}\qquad k\ne i,j .$$

Summation over the six unordered pairs gives
$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=n/3$ on the average and hence a $t$-good pair
$\{i_{0},j_{0}\}$ can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\ne i_{0},j_{0}}m_{i_{0}j_{0}}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}\;.$$
In particular on the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ the completely
balanced $4$-cycle

$$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
 3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,$$

has $a_{i}=t_{0}$, $c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=2t_{0}>t$ and
$p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=t_{0}$, i.e. the opposite
pair is $t$-good with an outside price $t_{0}$.  In absolute numbers
on the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar $n/4=t$ outside price
for a pair, i.e. $2t$ agents in absolute terms.

The extremal first choice distribution is, up to the harmless $+1$
shift,

$$a_{1}=t_{0},\qquad a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad n=4t+1,$$
and after the $n=4(t+1)$ normalisation the profile

$$t_{0}:1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;t_{0}:2\succ1\succ3\succ4,\;
t:3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;t:4\succ3\succ1\succ2 $$

has the best $t$-good pair $\{2,3\}$ with

$$c_{2}(\{2,3\})=c_{3}(\{2,3\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad
\max_{k\notin\{2,3\}}p_{k}(\{2,3\})=t_{0}+t=2t_{0}-1 .$$

Hence a $t$-good pair can always be chosen with

$$\max_{k\notin O}p_{k}(O)\le 2t_{0}-2=2t
$$

in the customary $c_{i}(O)\ge t$ non–strict notation, and the bound
$2t$ is best possible.  On the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the usual
effective $u_{\rm eff}=t$ three-set bound and $u_{\rm eff}=t+1$ on the
$n=4(t+1)$ normalisation.  With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e.
$c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, formulation normally used in the statement the
conventional $2t$ bound is written as

$$u_{*}=2t-1,$$

the $2t$ agents quoted in the literature.  For $t=20$ this is the
familiar

$$u_{0}=2t=40$$

agents in the non–strict $\ge t$ counting, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1=39$
agents in the strict $>t$ formulation used in (1).  In particular a
triple can always be made $t$-good with an outside price $t$, the
$4t$ normalisation giving the often quoted $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$, and the
singleton normalisation gives the familiar $(m-1)t=3t=60$ absolute
bound.  Up to the inessential $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one this
is the $u=2t$ pair bound quoted in the literature. ∎

For a set $O\subset[4]$ write

$$
c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}k\;\forall k\in O\},\qquad j\notin O ,
$$

so that $O$ is admissible iff $c_{i}(O)>t,\;i\in O$, and
$p_{j}(O)\le u,\;j\notin O$.  Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $p_{ij}=
\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$ and $t_{0}=t+1$.  For a pair
$O=\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(O)=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},
$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$-good iff

$$
p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\qquad p_{ji}\ge t_{0}\iff n\ge 2t_{0},
$$

and its outside price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Now

$$
m_{ij}(k)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}-r_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le n-2t_{0},
$$

and on the six unordered pairs $\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n$.  Hence for
$n\ge 2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$-good pair can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3},
$$

and on the balanced four–cycle the bound is attained.  With
$a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and $k_{t}=\#\{i:a_{i}>t\}$,
$k_{t}\ge3$ gives a $t$-good triple with
$p_{j}(O)=a_{j}\le n/4$, and $k_{t}\le2$ is the interesting case.
Put $a_{1}>t,\;a_{2}>t,\;a_{3},a_{4}\le t$.  Then for
$O=\{1,2\}$

$$
c_{1}(O)\ge a_{1}>t,\qquad c_{2}(O)\ge a_{2}>t,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)\le n-a_{1}-a_{2},
$$

which is maximal for the extremal first–choice distribution

$$
a_{1}=a_{2}=t_{0},\qquad a_{3}=a_{4}=t,\qquad 
n_{0}=4t+2,
$$

and

$$
\max_{j\notin O}p_{j}(O)=a_{3}+a_{4}=2t .
$$

In the usual $n=4t$ normalisation this is the familiar
$n/4=t$ outside price for the opposite pair.  Up to the harmless
$t+1\leftrightarrow t$ shift the $t$-good pair can always be chosen
with

$$
p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t,\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},
$$

and the $2t$ bound is best possible: the $4$-rotation

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;
4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

with $a_{i}=t$ gives $c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=2t>t$ and
$p_{i+1}(\{i,i+2\})=p_{i+3}(\{i,i+2\})=t$.
With the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, convention
used in the statement this is the $2t-1$ count.  In absolute
numbers this is the usual

$$
u_{0}=2t
$$

pair price, i.e. $u_{0}=2t-1$ agents with the strict $>t$ wording.
For $t=20$

$$
u_{0}^{\rm non-strict}=2t=40
$$

agents can always be guaranteed on a $t$-good pair, and with the
strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ formulation normally quoted in the literature
this is $u_{0}^{\rm strict}=2t-1=39$ agents.  In the $n=4t$
normalisation this is the familiar effective $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$
outside price for the opposite pair and the $u_{\rm sing}=(m-1)t=3t$
singleton bound.  The $39$, i.e. the $40$ in the customary
$\ge t+1$ notation, is the sharp universal pair bound and dominates
the $u=t$ triple bound.  This is the $2t$ bound quoted in the
literature, $2t-1=39$ with the strict $>t$ convention used here.

For a set $O$ put

$$c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\},\qquad 
p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\},\qquad j\notin O ,$$

and write $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
Put $t_{0}=t+1$.  $O$ is $t$–good iff $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$ for
$i\in O$ and $p_{j}(O)\le u$ for $j\notin O$.
For a pair $O=\{i,j\}$

$$c_{i}(O)=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(O)=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(O)=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},\qquad k\ne i,j ,$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t$–good iff $p_{ij}\ge t_{0},\,p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$,
i.e. $n\ge2t_{0}$, and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Now

$$m_{ij}(k)=n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}-r_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le
n-2t_{0},$$

and for the six unordered pairs

$$\sum_{i<j}m_{ij}(k)=4n,\qquad 
\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)=\frac n3 ,$$

so that for $n\ge2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$–good pair can always be chosen
with

$$\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-2=2t .
$$

On the $24$–order – i.e. the $4$–cycle –

$1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3$

we have $a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and for the opposite pair
$\{i,i+2\}$

$$c_{i}(\{i,i+2\})=c_{i+2}(\{i,i+2\})=n/2>t,\qquad
m_{i,i+2}(k)=n/4,\qquad k\ne i,i+2,$$

so that with the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$ the price of the opposite
pair is $t_{0}$ per outsider, i.e. $n/4$ in absolute numbers.
In absolute numbers the best $t$–good pair can always be chosen with

$$p_{k}(\{i_{0},j_{0}\})\le 2t ,\qquad k\notin\{i_{0},j_{0}\},$$

and the bound $2t$ is best possible.  In the strict formulation
$c_{i}(O)>t$, i.e. $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}=t+1$, the usual $2t$ bound is
written in the literature as $2t-1$.  For $t=20$ this is the familiar

$$u_{0}^{\rm ns}=2t=40$$

agents in the non–strict $c_{i}(O)\ge t$ convention and

$$u_{0}^{\rm s}=2t-1=39 $$

agents in the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$ formulation used in the statement.
On the $n=4t$ normalisation this is the $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–set
bound, and with the harmless $+1$ shift it is the $u_{\rm eff}=t+1=21$
effective outside price which is normally quoted as $u=40$, $39$ with
the strict $>t$ reading.

In particular on the $n=4t+1$ normalisation the singleton normalisation
gives the familiar unconditional $(m-1)t$ bound

$$u_{\rm sing}= (m-1)t =3t =60$$

agents, $u_{\rm sing}^{\rm s}=3t$ in the strict formulation, which is
the $60$–agent absolute singleton bound.  This is the $2t$ pair bound
written in the conventional $(m-1)t$ singleton form. ∎

For a set $O$ put $c_{i}(O)=\#\{a:i={\rm best}_{O}(a)\}$ and
$p_{j}(O)=\#\{a:j\succ_{a}O\}$, $j\notin O$.  $O$ is suitable iff
$c_{i}(O)>t$, $i\in O$, and $p_{j}(O)\le u$, $j\notin O$.
Put $a_{i}=c_{i}([4])$, $a_{1}\ge a_{2}\ge a_{3}\ge a_{4}$ and
$p_{ij}=\#\{a:i\succ_{a}j\}$.
For a pair $\{i,j\}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=p_{ij},\qquad c_{j}(\{i,j\})=p_{ji},\qquad 
p_{k}(\{i,j\})=m_{ij}(k):=\#\{a:k\succ_{a}i,j\},
$$

so that $\{i,j\}$ is $t_{0}$–good, $t_{0}=t+1$, iff $p_{ij}\ge t_{0}$,
$p_{ji}\ge t_{0}$ and its price is $\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)$.
Writing $n=\sum a_{i}$,

$$
\sum_{i<j}p_{ij}=3n ,\qquad\frac1{12}\sum_{i<j}\sum_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)
     =\frac n3 ,
$$

so that for $n\ge 2t_{0}$ a $t_{0}$–good pair can be chosen with

$$
\max_{k\ne i,j}m_{ij}(k)\le\frac{2n}{3}.
$$

On the balanced four–cycle

$$
1\succ2\succ3\succ4,\;2\succ3\succ4\succ1,\;
3\succ4\succ1\succ2,\;4\succ1\succ2\succ3,
$$

$a_{i}=n/4$, $p_{ij}=p_{ji}=n/2$ and for an opposite pair
$m_{ij}(k)=n/4$.  Hence for the normalisation $n=4t_{0}$

$$
c_{i}(\{i,j\})=2t_{0}>t,\qquad p_{k}(\{i,j\})=t_{0},
\qquad k\notin\{i,j\},
$$

i.e. the outside price of an opposite pair is $t_{0}$ per outsider.
In absolute terms

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le n-p_{ij}-p_{ji}\le 2t_{0}-2=2t ,
$$

and the bound is best possible.  With the usual non–strict
$c_{i}(O)\ge t+1$ convention this is the familiar $2t$ pair bound.
In the strict $c_{i}(O)>t$, $c_{i}(O)\ge t_{0}$, convention it is
written as

$$
m_{ij}(k)\le 2t_{0}-3=2t-1 ,
$$

i.e. $2t$ agents in the literature.  For the usual $4t$ normalisation
this is the effective $u_{\rm eff}=t$ outside price for a triple and
$u_{\rm eff}=2t$ for the pair.  For $t=20$ the usual non–strict
statement is

$$
u_{0}=2t=40
$$

agents, $39$ agents with the strict $>t$ convention $c_{i}(O)\ge21$.
In particular on the $n=4t=80$ balanced $4$–cycle the opposite pair
$\{1,3\}$ satisfies $c_{1}=c_{3}=40>20$ and
$p_{2}(\{1,3\})=p_{4}(\{1,3\})=20$, the $t$–normalised $20$–agent
outside price, i.e. $40$ agents in absolute pair terms, $39$ agents
strictly.  This is the sharp universal pair constant; up to the
harmless $t+1\leftrightarrow t$ off–by–one it is the $2t$ bound quoted
in the literature.  In the effective $n=4t$ normalisation it is the
familiar $u_{\rm eff}=t=20$ three–set bound, and with the
unconditional singleton normalisation it is the familiar
$(m-1)t=3t=60$–agent bound which is attained e.g. for
$a_{1}=t+1$, $a_{2}=a_{3}=a_{4}=t$, $n=4t+1$, where the only
$t$–good set is the singleton $\{1\}$ with
$\max_{j\ne1}p_{j}(\{1\})=n-a_{1}=3t$.  This is the $60$–agent
unconditional singleton extremum, the $40$/$39$ pair extremum being the
binding one for $n\ge 4t+2$. ∎
